claims.claim: Total cholesterol is the full amount of cholesterol travelling in your blood, counting both the helpful and the less helpful kinds together.
Cholesterol is a waxy fat your body needs to build cells and make some hormones and vitamin D.
Your liver makes most of it, and the rest comes from food.
Cholesterol cannot dissolve in blood, so it travels inside tiny carrier particles. LDL and HDL are the best known.
Too much cholesterol in the wrong carriers can slowly build up in artery walls and narrow them.
Total cholesterol is usually checked as part of a lipid profile to judge heart and blood vessel health.
A lower total is often a good sign for the heart. Very low values are uncommon and can occasionally go with an overactive thyroid, poor nutrition or some liver conditions.
Your total cholesterol is inside the lab's range. Heart risk still depends on how it is split between LDL and HDL, and on things like blood pressure, smoking and diabetes.

A higher total usually means more cholesterol is circulating. It may come from LDL, which can build up in arteries, or partly from HDL, which is helpful. Your LDL and HDL results show which one is driving it.
Your report did not include a reference range for total cholesterol, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Inherited cholesterol patterns: Genes set how much cholesterol your liver makes and how fast it clears LDL, so some people run high even with careful eating.
Foods high in saturated fat: Ghee, butter, cream, fatty meat and many fried snacks lead the liver to clear less LDL from the blood, which raises the total.
Body weight: Extra body fat, especially around the waist, tends to raise LDL and triglycerides and lower HDL.
Physical activity: Regular activity mainly lifts HDL and lowers triglycerides, which changes the mix inside the total.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid slows LDL clearance, so cholesterol can rise until the thyroid is treated.
Cholesterol-lowering medicines: Statins and similar medicines lower LDL, which brings the total down.

Many labs print a desirable cut-off rather than a range drawn from healthy people. The level a doctor aims for depends on your overall heart risk, including blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, so the same number can be fine for one person and too high for another.
A normal total does not always mean a healthy pattern. A high HDL can hide a raised LDL inside a normal-looking total, so the separate results matter more.
Thin people can have high cholesterol too, because genes play a large part.
Total cholesterol adds HDL and LDL together, so on its own it cannot show whether the cholesterol is mostly the helpful or the harmful kind.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Choose oils like mustard, groundnut or olive oil more often than ghee, butter or vanaspati. Unsaturated fats are kinder to blood cholesterol.
Add a bowl of dal, beans, oats or vegetables to most meals. Their fibre helps carry cholesterol out of your body.
Try to move for about 30 minutes on most days, such as a brisk walk. Regular activity helps raise HDL and lower other blood fats.
Foods rich in saturated fat, such as fatty meat, butter, ghee and many fried or packaged snacks, tend to raise blood cholesterol.
Soluble fibre from oats, dal, beans and fruit helps your body clear cholesterol.
Talk to a doctor if your cholesterol is high and you also have diabetes or high blood pressure.
Also talk to a doctor if a parent or sibling had a heart attack or stroke at a young age.
HDL is often called good cholesterol. This test measures how much cholesterol is carried by HDL particles, which help remove extra cholesterol from your body.
HDL particles pick up spare cholesterol from tissues and artery walls.
HDL carries it back to your liver, which clears it from your body.
This test measures how much cholesterol is inside HDL particles. It does not measure how well those particles are doing their clean-up work.
Low HDL is linked with a higher chance of heart disease.
Doctors look at HDL together with LDL and triglycerides to judge heart risk.
Low HDL means less cholesterol is being cleared away. It often goes with low activity, smoking, extra weight around the waist, high triglycerides or insulin resistance.
Your HDL is inside the healthy range, which is encouraging. It is still read together with your LDL, triglycerides and other heart risk factors, because a good HDL does not cancel out a high LDL.
Higher HDL is generally linked with lower heart risk. Very high levels, above about 100 mg/dL, do not add extra protection and in some people come from inherited patterns or heavy alcohol use.
Your report did not include a reference range for HDL (good cholesterol), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Physical activity: Regular aerobic activity such as brisk walking is one of the few habits shown to raise HDL.
Smoking: Smoking lowers HDL; stopping lets it recover.
Waist size and body weight: Extra fat around the waist goes with lower HDL; losing some of it can raise HDL a little.
Triglyceride levels: When triglycerides are high, HDL particles are reshaped and cleared faster, so HDL usually falls.
Inherited patterns: Genes strongly shape HDL, which is why some people have low or very high HDL despite their habits.
Some medicines: Some medicines, such as anabolic steroids and some blood pressure tablets, can lower HDL.
Healthy HDL is usually above 40 mg/dL for men and above 50 mg/dL for women. Some reports print one cut-off for everyone, so check which applies to you.
More HDL is not always better. Raising HDL with medicines has not lowered heart attacks, so doctors do not treat HDL as a target on its own.
HDL concentration is not the same as HDL working well. Two people with the same HDL number can have particles that clear cholesterol differently.
HDL measures the cholesterol inside HDL particles, not how well those particles work. A good HDL result does not cancel out a high LDL.
Regular activity and not smoking are the habits most linked with keeping HDL healthy.
If you do not drink alcohol, there is no reason to start to raise HDL.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Build movement into your day, such as walking after meals or taking stairs. Regular activity is one of the few habits known to lift HDL.
If you smoke, ask about support to stop. Stopping smoking helps HDL recover and protects your blood vessels.
Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour. They push triglycerides up, which usually pulls HDL down.
Regular physical activity and stopping smoking are among the most reliable ways HDL rises.
Diets high in refined carbohydrates and sugar tend to go with lower HDL and higher triglycerides.
Talk to a doctor if HDL is low alongside high LDL, high triglycerides, high blood sugar or high blood pressure, as these together raise heart risk.
Triglycerides are the most common type of fat in your blood. Your body stores spare energy from food as triglycerides and uses them as fuel between meals.
When you eat more energy than you need right away, your body turns the extra into triglycerides.
Triglycerides are stored in fat cells and released later when you need energy.
Sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol are easily turned into triglycerides by the liver.
High triglycerides are linked with heart disease, fatty liver and insulin resistance.
Very high levels can inflame the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach that helps digestion.
Low triglycerides are usually not a concern. They can go with a low-fat diet, regular exercise, and occasionally an overactive thyroid or poor absorption of food.
Your triglycerides are inside the lab's range, which suggests your body is handling fats from food well at the moment.
Higher triglycerides often reflect a recent meal, extra sugar or refined carbohydrates, alcohol, extra weight or insulin resistance. If you did not fast before the test, the result can read higher.
Your report did not include a reference range for triglycerides, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Recent meal or not fasting: Fat from a meal travels in the blood as triglycerides for some hours, which is why you may be asked to fast for 9 to 12 hours before this test.
Sugar and refined carbohydrates: When you eat more sugar or refined flour than you burn, your liver turns the extra into triglycerides.
Alcohol: Alcohol is turned into fat by the liver and can push triglycerides up sharply, even in moderate amounts for some people.
Body weight: Extra weight, especially around the waist, goes with higher triglycerides.
Insulin resistance or diabetes: When insulin works poorly, the liver makes more triglyceride-rich particles and the body clears them more slowly.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid can slow how quickly triglycerides are cleared.

Many labs print a desirable cut-off rather than a range drawn from healthy people. The level a doctor aims for depends on your overall heart risk, including blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, so the same number can be fine for one person and too high for another.
Triglycerides are not only about fatty food. Sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol often raise them more.
Triglycerides change a lot after eating and drinking alcohol, so one result may not reflect your usual level.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Triglycerides respond quickly to cutting sugary drinks, sweets, refined flour and alcohol, often within weeks.
Very high triglycerides, roughly above 500 mg/dL, can inflame the pancreas, so they need prompt medical advice.
Swap sugary drinks and packaged juices for water, buttermilk or unsweetened tea. Liquid sugar is turned into triglycerides quickly.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and choose smaller portions of rice, roti or bread. This lowers the sugar load your liver has to process.
Keep alcohol low or avoid it. Even small amounts can raise triglycerides in some people.
Walk for 10 to 15 minutes after main meals. Moving muscles use blood fats and sugar as fuel.
Sweets, sugary drinks, white rice and maida-based foods in large amounts can raise triglycerides.
Alcohol raises triglycerides strongly in some people, even in modest amounts.
Regular activity helps your muscles burn triglycerides for fuel.
See a doctor soon if your triglycerides are very high, especially with tummy pain, as very high levels can inflame the pancreas.
Talk to a doctor if triglycerides are high along with high blood sugar or signs of fatty liver.
Non-HDL cholesterol is your total cholesterol minus your HDL. It shows all the cholesterol carried in particles that can build up in artery walls.
Several kinds of carrier particles, including LDL and VLDL, can leave cholesterol in artery walls.
Non-HDL adds all of these together into one number.
Non-HDL cholesterol is calculated from your results, so no extra blood is needed.
Non-HDL can be a better guide to heart risk than LDL alone, especially when triglycerides are high.
Non-HDL cholesterol is still reliable if you had eaten before the test.
A lower non-HDL is generally favourable for heart health.
Your non-HDL cholesterol is inside the lab's range, which suggests the amount of plaque-forming cholesterol is not raised.
A higher non-HDL means more cholesterol is in particles that can narrow arteries. It usually rises with high LDL or high triglycerides.
Your report did not include a reference range for non-HDL cholesterol, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
LDL cholesterol: Non-HDL includes LDL, so anything that raises LDL raises non-HDL.
Triglyceride levels: Non-HDL also includes VLDL and remnant particles, which carry triglycerides, so high triglycerides lift it.
Foods high in saturated fat: These lead the liver to clear less LDL, which raises non-HDL.
Inherited patterns: Genes shape how many plaque-forming particles your liver makes and clears.
Cholesterol-lowering medicines: Statins and similar medicines lower LDL and so lower non-HDL.

Many labs print a desirable cut-off rather than a range drawn from healthy people. The level a doctor aims for depends on your overall heart risk, including blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, so the same number can be fine for one person and too high for another.
Non-HDL does not need a fasting sample to be useful, which is one reason doctors like it.
Non-HDL is calculated from other results, so any error in total cholesterol or HDL carries through to it.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Cut down on fried snacks, sweets and fatty meat. They feed both LDL and triglycerides, the two parts of non-HDL.
Eat more fibre from dal, oats, beans, fruit and vegetables. Fibre helps remove cholesterol from your body.
Aim for regular activity most days. It lowers triglycerides and supports healthy cholesterol.
The same habits that lower LDL and triglycerides, such as less saturated fat, less sugar and more activity, also lower non-HDL cholesterol.
Talk to a doctor if non-HDL is high, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking or early heart disease in your family.
This ratio divides your total cholesterol by your HDL (good cholesterol). It gives a quick sense of how much of your cholesterol is the helpful kind.
A smaller number means a larger share of your cholesterol is HDL.
A bigger number means less HDL compared with the total.
The ratio is worked out from your two results and is not a separate blood measurement.
Doctors sometimes use this ratio as one simple pointer to heart risk alongside other results.
A lower ratio means HDL makes up a good share of your cholesterol, which is generally favourable.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range, suggesting a reasonable balance between total cholesterol and HDL.
A higher ratio means HDL makes up a smaller share of your cholesterol. This is linked with higher heart risk, usually because LDL is high, HDL is low, or both.
Your report did not include a reference range for total cholesterol to HDL ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Total cholesterol: A ratio moves when either part moves, so a change in Total cholesterol shifts the ratio even if HDL cholesterol stays the same.
HDL cholesterol: Likewise a change in HDL cholesterol shifts the ratio; looking at the two results separately shows which one moved.
A ratio cannot replace the separate results. Two very different cholesterol patterns can give the same ratio.
A ratio can look fine even when both numbers are high, so the separate cholesterol results still matter.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Talk to a doctor if the ratio is high together with other heart risk factors such as diabetes or high blood pressure.
LDL is often called bad cholesterol. This result estimates how much cholesterol is carried by LDL particles, the main type that builds up in artery walls.
LDL particles deliver cholesterol to cells around your body.
When there are too many, some get trapped in artery walls and form fatty deposits called plaque.
Plaque can slowly narrow arteries and reduce blood flow to the heart and brain.
LDL is the main cholesterol target doctors use to judge and treat heart risk.
This lab calculates LDL from your other cholesterol results instead of measuring it directly.
A lower LDL is generally good for heart health. Very low values are uncommon and may be checked if there is a medical reason.
Your LDL is inside the lab's range. The healthy target for you can be lower if you have diabetes, kidney disease or existing heart disease, so a doctor may set a personal goal.

A higher LDL means more cholesterol is available to build up in arteries. Diet, weight, inherited patterns and other conditions can all raise it. Very high values can point to an inherited cholesterol condition.
Your report did not include a reference range for LDL (calculated bad cholesterol), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Foods high in saturated and trans fat: Saturated fat (ghee, butter, cream, fatty meat) and trans fat (some fried and bakery foods, vanaspati) lead the liver to clear less LDL.
Inherited patterns: Some families carry genes that slow LDL clearance, giving very high LDL from a young age.
Body weight: Extra weight tends to raise LDL a little; the effect is larger on triglycerides and HDL.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid slows LDL clearance.
Kidney or liver conditions: Some kidney conditions that leak protein, and blocked bile flow, can raise LDL.
Cholesterol-lowering medicines: Statins and similar medicines lower LDL substantially.

Many labs print a desirable cut-off rather than a range drawn from healthy people. The level a doctor aims for depends on your overall heart risk, including blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, so the same number can be fine for one person and too high for another.
Feeling well does not mean LDL is fine. High LDL causes no symptoms while it builds up in arteries.
This LDL is usually calculated from other results, not measured directly, so it can be less accurate when triglycerides are very high.
Calculated LDL is less accurate when triglycerides are very high or LDL is very low, and it does not show the number of LDL particles.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Soluble fibre from oats, dal, rajma, chana and fruit helps the body remove some cholesterol.
Swapping ghee, butter and fried snacks for small amounts of mustard, groundnut or olive oil and nuts lowers LDL.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
Cook with less ghee, butter and vanaspati, and use plant oils in small amounts instead. This lowers the saturated and trans fat that raise LDL.
Eat oats, dal, rajma, chana or barley several times a week. Their soluble fibre binds cholesterol in the gut.
Have a small handful of unsalted nuts most days in place of fried snacks. Nuts contain fats that can help LDL.
Keep active and work towards a healthy waist size. Both help LDL and overall heart health.
Saturated fat from ghee, butter, cream, fatty meat and many bakery and fried foods raises LDL.
Trans fats in vanaspati and some packaged snacks raise LDL and lower HDL.
Soluble fibre and nuts can help lower LDL modestly.
Talk to a doctor if LDL is high, especially if you have diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease or family members who had heart problems young.
Very high LDL can be inherited and may need medical treatment, as diet alone is often not enough.
VLDL cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in very low-density lipoprotein, a particle your liver makes to carry triglycerides (blood fats) around your body.
Your liver packs triglycerides into VLDL particles and sends them into your blood.
As they release fat to your tissues, VLDL particles shrink and can turn into LDL.
Most labs estimate VLDL from your triglyceride result rather than measuring it directly.
VLDL gives an extra view of how many fat-carrying particles your liver is making, which is linked with heart risk.
Low VLDL is usually not a concern and generally matches low triglycerides.
Your VLDL is inside the lab's range, which usually matches healthy triglyceride levels.
Higher VLDL usually goes with high triglycerides. It often reflects extra sugar or refined carbohydrates, alcohol, extra weight or insulin resistance.
Your report did not include a reference range for VLDL cholesterol, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Triglyceride levels: VLDL is usually estimated from triglycerides, so it rises and falls with them.
Sugar and refined carbohydrates: Extra sugar is turned into triglycerides, which the liver packs into VLDL.
Alcohol: Alcohol makes the liver produce more VLDL.
Body weight: Extra weight goes with more VLDL production.
Insulin resistance or diabetes: When insulin works poorly, the liver releases more VLDL.
VLDL on most reports is calculated from triglycerides, so it adds little new information on its own.
VLDL is usually estimated from triglycerides, so it adds little information beyond the triglyceride result and is less reliable when triglycerides are very high.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Limit sweets, sugary drinks and refined flour. Your liver turns extra sugar into the fat that VLDL carries.
Keep alcohol low or avoid it. Alcohol increases the fat your liver sends out in VLDL.
Stay active on most days. Active muscles take up and burn blood fats.
VLDL follows triglycerides closely, so cutting back on sugar, refined flour and alcohol and staying active usually lowers both.
Talk to a doctor if VLDL and triglycerides are both high, particularly with high blood sugar or a large waist.
This ratio compares your LDL (bad cholesterol) with your HDL (good cholesterol). It shows how much plaque-forming cholesterol you have for each unit of the helpful kind.
A higher number means more LDL compared with HDL.
The ratio is calculated from your two cholesterol results, not measured separately.
The ratio is a simple way to see the balance between cholesterol that builds up in arteries and cholesterol that is cleared away.
A lower ratio means HDL is strong compared with LDL, which is generally favourable.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range, suggesting a reasonable balance between LDL and HDL.
A higher ratio means LDL is high compared with HDL. This balance is linked with higher heart risk.
Your report did not include a reference range for LDL to HDL ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
LDL cholesterol: A ratio moves when either part moves, so a change in LDL cholesterol shifts the ratio even if HDL cholesterol stays the same.
HDL cholesterol: Likewise a change in HDL cholesterol shifts the ratio; looking at the two results separately shows which one moved.
A ratio cannot replace the separate results. Two very different cholesterol patterns can give the same ratio.
The ratio can hide a high LDL if HDL is also high, so the separate results still need to be read.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Talk to a doctor if the ratio is high along with diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of early heart disease.
This ratio compares your HDL (good cholesterol) with your LDL (bad cholesterol). It is the LDL to HDL ratio turned the other way up, so here a higher number is better.
A higher number means you have more HDL for each unit of LDL.
The ratio is calculated from your two cholesterol results.
The ratio shows the same balance as the LDL to HDL ratio, just expressed the other way round.
A lower ratio means LDL is high compared with HDL. This balance is linked with higher heart risk.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range, suggesting a reasonable balance between HDL and LDL.
A higher ratio means HDL is strong compared with LDL, which is generally favourable for the heart.
Your report did not include a reference range for HDL to LDL ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
HDL cholesterol: A ratio moves when either part moves, so a change in HDL cholesterol shifts the ratio even if LDL cholesterol stays the same.
LDL cholesterol: Likewise a change in LDL cholesterol shifts the ratio; looking at the two results separately shows which one moved.
A ratio cannot replace the separate results. Two very different cholesterol patterns can give the same ratio.
Because this ratio is the reverse of the LDL to HDL ratio, it does not add new information. The separate results matter most.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Talk to a doctor if the ratio is low along with other heart risk factors.
Albumin is the main protein in your blood. It is made by your liver and helps keep fluid in your blood vessels.
Albumin acts like a sponge that holds water inside your blood vessels, so it does not leak into tissues.
Albumin also carries hormones, vitamins, calcium and some medicines around your body.
Your liver makes albumin every day, so its level reflects liver work, nutrition and losses from the body.
Albumin helps doctors check liver function, nutrition and whether protein is being lost through the kidneys or gut.
Low albumin can happen during illness or inflammation, with liver disease, with protein loss through the kidneys or gut, or with poor nutrition. Low levels can cause swelling in the legs or tummy.
Your albumin is inside the lab's range, which suggests your liver is making enough of this protein and you are not losing large amounts.
High albumin is uncommon and most often means you were a little dehydrated when the sample was taken, which concentrates the blood.
Your report did not include a reference range for albumin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: When you are short of water the blood is more concentrated, so albumin reads higher; extra fluid dilutes it.
Recent illness or inflammation: During illness the liver switches to making infection-fighting proteins and makes less albumin.
Liver function: Albumin is made only in the liver, so long-term liver disease can lower it.
Protein loss through kidneys: Damaged kidney filters can leak albumin into urine, lowering the blood level.
Nutrition: Very low protein intake over a long time can lower albumin, though illness is a more common cause.
Low albumin is not usually fixed by protein powder. It more often reflects illness, liver or kidney problems that need a doctor to find.
Albumin changes slowly, over about three weeks, so it does not reflect very recent changes in nutrition.
Eating some protein at each meal, such as dal, curd, paneer, eggs, fish or chicken, gives the liver what it needs to make albumin.
Drink enough water through the day, especially in hot weather. Dehydration can make albumin read high.
Include a protein food at each meal, such as dal, eggs, curd, paneer, fish or chicken. Your liver needs protein to build albumin.
Long-term low protein intake can lower albumin, but in most people low albumin is caused by illness rather than diet.
See a doctor if albumin is low, especially with swelling of the legs, ankles or tummy, frothy urine, or weight loss.
Alkaline phosphatase, or ALP, is an enzyme found mainly in your liver, bile ducts and bones. An enzyme is a protein that helps chemical reactions happen.
ALP is an enzyme, a protein that speeds up chemical reactions. It is found mainly in the liver, the bile ducts and bone.
Small amounts leak into your blood all the time.
More enters your blood when bile ducts are blocked, or when bone-building cells are busy, as in growing children or a healing fracture.
ALP is also normally higher during pregnancy, which has nothing to do with bone-building.
ALP helps spot problems with bile flow from the liver, and some bone conditions.

Low ALP is uncommon. It can go with poor nutrition or low protein, low zinc, thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia (a condition that stops B12 being absorbed), Wilson disease, or a rare inherited bone condition called hypophosphatasia. It is worth mentioning to a doctor rather than ignoring.
Your ALP is inside the lab's range, suggesting no sign of bile flow problems or unusual bone activity from this test.

Higher ALP may come from the liver or bile ducts, for example when bile cannot flow freely, or from bone, for example during growth, healing or bone softening from long-term low vitamin D. An overactive thyroid or parathyroid gland can also raise it, and it is normally higher in pregnancy. Your GGT result helps tell whether the liver or bone is the more likely source.
Your report did not include a reference range for alkaline phosphatase (ALP), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Bone growth or healing: Bone-building cells release ALP, so growing children and teenagers, and people healing a fracture, have higher levels.
Bile duct problems: When bile cannot flow freely, the cells lining the bile ducts release more ALP into the blood.
Pregnancy: ALP is normally higher during pregnancy, separate from any bone or liver cause, so results in pregnancy are judged against pregnancy ranges.
Vitamin D levels: A long shortage of vitamin D can soften bones (osteomalacia), which is one cause of a high ALP.
Thyroid and parathyroid glands: An overactive thyroid or parathyroid gland speeds up bone turnover and can raise ALP.
Some medicines: Some medicines can affect the liver or bile flow and raise ALP.
A high ALP does not always mean a liver problem. In children, teenagers and pregnant women it is often expected, and in adults it may come from bone.
ALP alone cannot tell whether the extra enzyme comes from the liver or from bone. GGT or other tests are needed for that.
See a doctor if ALP is high along with yellowing of the eyes or skin, itching, dark urine, pale stools or bone pain.
Direct bilirubin is the part of bilirubin that your liver has already processed and is ready to send out of your body in bile.
When old red blood cells break down, they release a yellow pigment called bilirubin.
Your liver changes it into a water-friendly form called direct bilirubin.
Direct bilirubin flows out with bile into the gut and leaves your body in stool.
A high direct bilirubin suggests a problem with how bile drains out of the liver, rather than with red blood cells breaking down.
A low direct bilirubin is not a concern.
Your direct bilirubin is inside the lab's range, which suggests your liver is processing and draining bilirubin normally.

Higher direct bilirubin can mean bile is not draining well, for example from a gallstone blocking a bile duct, swelling of the liver, or a liver condition. It can cause yellow skin or eyes and dark urine.
Your report did not include a reference range for direct bilirubin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Bile duct blockage such as gallstones: A stone or narrowing stops processed bilirubin draining into the gut, so it backs up into the blood.
Liver inflammation: Inflamed liver cells cannot pass processed bilirubin into bile as well, so more leaks into the blood.
Some medicines: A few medicines slow bile flow inside the liver and raise direct bilirubin.
Yellow eyes are not always from eating too much oily food. When direct bilirubin is high, a doctor needs to check the bile ducts and liver.
Direct bilirubin is measured with a lab method that does not perfectly match the processed form, so small differences between labs are normal.
See a doctor promptly if direct bilirubin is high, or if you notice yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, pale stools, itching or pain in the upper right tummy.
Total bilirubin measures all the bilirubin in your blood. Bilirubin is a yellow pigment made when old red blood cells are broken down.
Your body replaces red blood cells every few months, and the old ones are broken down.
Breaking them down releases bilirubin, which your liver processes and sends out in bile.
If too much is made, or the liver cannot clear it, bilirubin builds up and can turn the skin and eyes yellow.
Bilirubin helps check how well your liver is clearing waste and whether red blood cells are breaking down faster than usual.
Low bilirubin is not a health concern.
Your total bilirubin is inside the lab's range, suggesting your liver is clearing this pigment as expected.

Higher bilirubin can come from red cells breaking down faster, from liver problems, or from blocked bile flow. A common cause that is not dangerous is Gilbert syndrome, an inherited pattern where bilirubin rises a little, especially with fasting, poor sleep or illness.
Your report did not include a reference range for total bilirubin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Red blood cell breakdown: Bilirubin comes from old red cells, so faster breakdown produces more of it.
Liver function: The liver processes bilirubin; when it is struggling, bilirubin builds up.
Bile flow: Blocked bile ducts stop processed bilirubin leaving the body, so it backs up into the blood.
Gilbert syndrome: A common inherited pattern in which the liver processes bilirubin a little slowly. It is not dangerous.
Fasting or recent illness: In people with Gilbert syndrome, fasting, poor sleep or illness can raise bilirubin for a while.
Gilbert syndrome is not liver disease. It is a common inherited pattern that does not damage the liver.
Total bilirubin does not show the cause. The direct and indirect parts help tell whether the liver, bile ducts or red cells are involved.
Eat regular meals rather than skipping them, if your bilirubin is mildly high. In people with Gilbert syndrome, long gaps without food can raise it.
Long fasting and illness can raise bilirubin a little in people with Gilbert syndrome.
See a doctor if bilirubin is high together with yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, tummy pain or tiredness.
Gamma-glutamyl transferase, or GGT, is an enzyme found mostly in the liver and bile ducts. It rises when the liver or bile ducts are under strain.
GGT helps your cells move substances in and out and handle protective molecules.
When liver cells or bile ducts are irritated, more GGT spills into your blood.
Alcohol and some medicines can make the liver produce more GGT.
GGT is a sensitive sign of liver or bile duct strain, and it helps tell whether a high ALP comes from the liver or from bone.
A low GGT is not a concern.
Your GGT is inside the lab's range, suggesting no sign of liver or bile duct strain from this test.
Higher GGT can reflect alcohol use, fatty liver, bile duct problems or some medicines. It is sensitive but not specific, so it shows strain without saying exactly why.
Your report did not include a reference range for gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Alcohol: Regular drinking makes liver cells produce more GGT, so it often rises with alcohol use and falls after stopping.
Fatty liver: Fat building up in the liver raises GGT, often along with ALT.
Bile duct problems: GGT sits in the cells lining the bile ducts and rises when bile does not drain freely.
Some medicines: Some medicines, such as certain seizure medicines, make the liver produce more GGT.
Body weight: Extra weight goes with fat in the liver, which raises GGT.
GGT is not only an alcohol test. Fatty liver, bile duct problems and medicines raise it too.
A high GGT shows liver or bile duct strain but cannot identify the cause on its own.
Keep doing what protects your liver: little or no alcohol, few sugary drinks and sweets, regular activity and a steady weight.
Ask before starting herbal, weight-loss or bodybuilding supplements. Some herbal and dietary supplements can injure the liver.
About one in three Indian adults has fat in the liver, often without being overweight, so keeping sugar, refined flour and alcohol low is worth it even when you feel well.
Losing 3 to 5% of body weight can reduce liver fat, and regular activity helps the liver even when weight does not change.
Keep alcohol low or avoid it. Your liver has to break down every drink, and alcohol is a common cause of liver strain.
Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets and fried foods. Extra sugar and fat can build up in the liver.
Stay active and work towards a healthy waist size. Losing even a little extra weight can reduce fat in the liver.
GGT often rises with regular alcohol use and with fat building up in the liver.
Talk to a doctor if GGT is high, especially with other abnormal liver tests, yellow eyes or skin, or tummy pain.
Total protein measures all the protein in the liquid part of your blood. It is mainly made up of albumin and globulins.
Albumin keeps fluid in your blood vessels and carries substances around your body.
Globulins include antibodies that fight infection, as well as carrier and clotting proteins.
Your liver makes albumin and many globulins. Immune cells make antibodies.
Total protein gives a broad picture of nutrition, liver function, kidney losses and immune activity.
Lower total protein can come from liver disease, protein loss through the kidneys or gut, poor nutrition or problems absorbing food.
Your total protein is inside the lab's range, suggesting a normal overall balance of blood proteins.
Higher total protein can come from dehydration, ongoing inflammation or infection, or, less often, from a condition where the immune system makes too much of one antibody.
Your report did not include a reference range for total blood protein, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises total protein; extra fluid dilutes it.
Inflammation or infection: Long-term inflammation raises antibodies (globulins), which lifts total protein.
Liver function: The liver makes albumin, the largest part of total protein, so liver disease can lower it.
Protein loss through kidneys: Kidney filters that leak protein lower the blood level.
Nutrition: Very poor nutrition over a long time can lower total protein.
Total protein does not show how much protein you eat. It mostly reflects albumin and antibodies made by your body.
Total protein does not show which protein has changed. The albumin and globulin results show that.
Include a protein food at each meal, such as dal, curd, eggs, paneer, soya, fish or chicken. Your body needs protein to build blood proteins.
Drink enough fluids through the day. Dehydration can make protein read high.
Very low protein intake over a long time can lower blood protein, but illness is a more common cause.
Talk to a doctor if total protein is high or low, especially with swelling, weight loss, frequent infections or bone pain.
Aspartate aminotransferase, or AST, is an enzyme found in the liver and also in muscles, including the heart. It leaks into the blood when these cells are damaged.
AST helps your cells turn food into energy.
Healthy cells keep most of it inside. When liver or muscle cells are hurt, more AST spills into your blood.
Because muscles also contain AST, hard exercise or a muscle injury can raise it.
AST is used with ALT to check for liver cell damage. Comparing the two can give clues about the cause.
A low AST is not a concern.
Your AST is inside the lab's range, suggesting no sign of liver or muscle cell damage from this test.
Higher AST can come from liver strain, such as fatty liver, alcohol, hepatitis or some medicines. It can also rise after intense exercise or a muscle injury.
Your report did not include a reference range for aspartate aminotransferase (AST), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Fatty liver: Fat in liver cells stresses them, so more AST leaks out.
Alcohol: Alcohol damages liver cells and tends to raise AST more than ALT.
Hepatitis: Viral infections of the liver inflame liver cells and release AST.
Intense exercise: Hard workouts strain muscles, which also contain AST, so levels can rise for a day or two.
Muscle injury: Injured muscle releases AST into the blood.
Some medicines: Some medicines and supplements can strain the liver and raise AST.
Normal liver enzymes do not rule out fatty liver. A good share of people with fat in the liver have normal ALT and AST.
A high AST is not always the liver. Muscles contain AST too, so a recent hard workout can raise it.
AST is not specific to the liver, so a raised level may come from muscle rather than liver.
Keep doing what protects your liver: little or no alcohol, few sugary drinks and sweets, regular activity and a steady weight.
Ask before starting herbal, weight-loss or bodybuilding supplements. Some herbal and dietary supplements can injure the liver.
About one in three Indian adults has fat in the liver, often without being overweight, so keeping sugar, refined flour and alcohol low is worth it even when you feel well.
Losing 3 to 5% of body weight can reduce liver fat, and regular activity helps the liver even when weight does not change.
Keep alcohol low or avoid it. Your liver has to break down every drink, and alcohol is a common cause of liver strain.
Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets and fried foods. Extra sugar and fat can build up in the liver.
Avoid very hard workouts for a day or two before a blood test. Intense exercise can raise AST from your muscles.
Alcohol and extra body fat that builds up in the liver are common reasons AST rises.
See a doctor if AST is clearly high, keeps rising, or comes with yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, tummy pain or unusual tiredness.
Alanine aminotransferase, or ALT, is an enzyme found mainly in the liver. A high level in the blood is one of the clearest signs that liver cells are under strain.
ALT helps liver cells turn food into energy.
When liver cells are irritated or damaged, ALT leaks into the blood.
Because most ALT is in the liver, it is more liver-specific than AST.
ALT is the main blood test for spotting liver cell strain, which often has no symptoms early on.
A low ALT is not a concern.
Your ALT is inside the lab's range, suggesting no sign of liver cell strain from this test. Fatty liver can sometimes be present with a normal ALT.
Higher ALT usually means liver cells are under strain. Common causes include fat building up in the liver, alcohol, viral hepatitis and some medicines or supplements.
Your report did not include a reference range for alanine aminotransferase (ALT), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Fatty liver: Fat in liver cells is the most common reason ALT rises in India.
Alcohol: Alcohol damages liver cells and releases ALT.
Viral hepatitis: Hepatitis B and C infect liver cells and can raise ALT for years.
Body weight: Extra weight, especially around the waist, goes with fat in the liver.
Some medicines and supplements: Some medicines and herbal or dietary supplements can injure liver cells.
Normal liver enzymes do not rule out fatty liver. A good share of people with fat in the liver have normal ALT and AST.
The size of the ALT rise does not show how serious liver disease is.
A normal ALT does not fully rule out liver disease, and the level does not always match how serious the problem is.
Keep doing what protects your liver: little or no alcohol, few sugary drinks and sweets, regular activity and a steady weight.
Ask before starting herbal, weight-loss or bodybuilding supplements. Some herbal and dietary supplements can injure the liver.
About one in three Indian adults has fat in the liver, often without being overweight, so keeping sugar, refined flour and alcohol low is worth it even when you feel well.
Losing 3 to 5% of body weight can reduce liver fat, and regular activity helps the liver even when weight does not change.
Keep alcohol low or avoid it. Your liver has to break down every drink, and alcohol is a common cause of liver strain.
Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets and fried foods. Extra sugar and fat can build up in the liver.
Stay active and work towards a healthy waist size. Losing even a little extra weight can reduce fat in the liver.
Do not start herbal or bodybuilding supplements without advice. Some can harm the liver.
Extra weight, a diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrates, and alcohol can all lead to fat in the liver, which raises ALT.
See a doctor if ALT is high, especially if it stays high on a repeat test or you notice yellow eyes, dark urine, tummy pain or tiredness.
Indirect bilirubin is the part of bilirubin that has not yet been processed by your liver. It is worked out by subtracting direct bilirubin from total bilirubin.
When red blood cells break down, they release bilirubin into the blood first in this unprocessed form.
The liver then picks it up and changes it so it can leave the body.
A high indirect bilirubin points towards red cells breaking down faster, or a slower liver uptake such as in Gilbert syndrome.
Low indirect bilirubin is not a concern.
Your indirect bilirubin is inside the lab's range, suggesting normal red cell breakdown and liver uptake.
Higher indirect bilirubin can happen when red blood cells break down faster than usual, or with Gilbert syndrome, a common and harmless inherited pattern. Fasting or illness can make it rise.
Your report did not include a reference range for indirect bilirubin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Red blood cell breakdown: When red cells break down faster, more unprocessed bilirubin is made than the liver can handle at once.
Gilbert syndrome: In Gilbert syndrome the liver processes bilirubin slowly, so the unprocessed part rises a little.
Fasting or illness: Long gaps without food, poor sleep or illness raise it in people with Gilbert syndrome.
A mildly high indirect bilirubin with normal liver enzymes is often Gilbert syndrome, which is not dangerous.
Indirect bilirubin is calculated from two other results, so small errors in either one affect it.
Eat regular meals rather than going long hours without food, if indirect bilirubin is mildly high. Long gaps can raise it in Gilbert syndrome.
In Gilbert syndrome, long fasting or illness can raise indirect bilirubin a little.
Talk to a doctor if indirect bilirubin is high together with tiredness, breathlessness, pale skin or yellow eyes, which can point to faster red cell breakdown.
Globulins are a group of blood proteins that include antibodies, which fight infection, as well as proteins that carry substances and help blood clot.
Immune cells make antibodies, a major type of globulin.
The liver makes many other globulins.
Globulin is usually calculated as total protein minus albumin.
Globulin helps show immune activity and liver function. It is also used to work out the albumin to globulin ratio.
Lower globulin can happen when the body makes fewer antibodies, with liver disease, or when protein is lost through the kidneys or gut.
Your globulin is inside the lab's range, suggesting a normal level of these immune and carrier proteins.
Higher globulin often reflects ongoing inflammation or infection. Less often, it can be due to liver disease or a condition where the immune system makes too much of one antibody.
Your report did not include a reference range for globulin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Inflammation or infection: Long-lasting infection or inflammation makes the immune system produce more antibodies, which are globulins.
Immune conditions: Autoimmune conditions can raise antibody levels.
Liver function: Long-term liver disease can raise globulins while albumin falls.
Protein loss: Losing protein through the kidneys or gut can lower globulins.
Globulin is not one protein. It is a group, including antibodies, so a high result needs more tests to see which part is raised.
Globulin is a combined group, so it cannot show which protein has changed. Further tests are needed for that.
Talk to a doctor if globulin is high or low, especially with frequent infections, weight loss, bone pain or swelling.
The albumin to globulin ratio compares the two main groups of blood proteins. It is worked out from your albumin and globulin results.
Usually there is a little more albumin than globulin in the blood.
The ratio changes if one group rises or falls more than the other.
A change in the ratio can be a clue to inflammation, liver disease, kidney protein loss or an immune problem.
A lower ratio usually means globulin is high, for example with inflammation, or albumin is low, for example with liver disease or protein loss.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range, suggesting a normal balance between albumin and globulin.
A higher ratio usually means globulin is lower than usual. It is less common and is often not significant on its own.
Your report did not include a reference range for albumin to globulin ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Albumin level: A lower albumin, from illness, liver or kidney problems, pulls the ratio down.
Globulin level: Higher antibody levels, from long-term inflammation or immune conditions, also pull the ratio down.
The ratio adds little when albumin and globulin are both normal.
The ratio is calculated from two other results and does not show which protein has changed.
Talk to a doctor if the ratio is abnormal along with other abnormal liver or kidney results.
The AST to ALT ratio compares two liver enzymes. The pattern can give clues about what is affecting the liver.
AST is found in the liver and in muscle, while ALT is found mainly in the liver.
The ratio is worked out from your two results.
When liver enzymes are raised, the ratio can help a doctor think about possible causes, such as fatty liver or alcohol.
A lower ratio means ALT is higher than AST, a pattern often seen with fatty liver or viral hepatitis.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range. The ratio matters most when AST or ALT is raised.
A higher ratio means AST is high compared with ALT. This pattern can be seen with alcohol-related liver strain, advanced liver scarring or muscle sources of AST.
Your report did not include a reference range for AST to ALT ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
AST level: AST rises with alcohol-related liver damage, scarring and muscle strain, which pushes the ratio up.
ALT level: ALT rises most with fatty liver and viral hepatitis, which pushes the ratio down.
The ratio is not a diagnosis. It only hints at a pattern when AST or ALT is raised.
The ratio means little when both enzymes are normal, and it can be misleading when one value is very low.
Talk to a doctor if AST or ALT is raised, as the ratio helps guide what to check next.
Blood urea nitrogen, or BUN, measures urea in your blood. Urea is a waste product made when your body breaks down protein, and your kidneys remove it.
When your body uses protein, it makes ammonia, which the liver turns into urea.
Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys, which filter it out into urine.
If the kidneys filter less well, or you are dehydrated, urea builds up in the blood.
BUN is one of the basic checks of kidney function and hydration, usually read with creatinine.
Lower BUN can come from a low-protein diet, drinking a lot of fluid, pregnancy or, less often, liver disease.
Your BUN is inside the lab's range, suggesting your kidneys are clearing protein waste as expected.
Higher BUN often means you were dehydrated, ate a lot of protein, or have bleeding in the stomach or gut. It can also mean the kidneys are filtering less well.
Your report did not include a reference range for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Being short of water concentrates the blood and slows kidney filtering for a while, so this result can read higher; it settles once you drink normally.
Protein intake: Urea nitrogen is made when the body breaks down protein, so a high-protein diet raises it a little and a very low one lowers it.
Kidney function: Healthy kidneys keep this level steady; when filtering falls, the level drifts out of range.
Bleeding in the gut: Blood digested in the gut is a large protein load, which raises BUN.
Liver function: The liver makes urea, so severe liver disease can lower BUN.
Some medicines: Steroids and some antibiotics can raise BUN.
A high BUN on its own does not mean kidney failure. Dehydration is a very common reason, which is why it is read with creatinine.
BUN is affected by diet and hydration, so it is less reliable than creatinine or eGFR for judging kidney function.
Keep blood pressure and blood sugar in a healthy range. They are the two most common causes of kidney damage.
Drink water through the day, more in heat or after sweating, and use painkillers such as ibuprofen or diclofenac only as advised.
Drink water regularly through the day, more in hot weather or after sweating. Good hydration helps your kidneys and keeps results reliable.
Dehydration and a very high-protein diet can both raise BUN.
Talk to a doctor if kidney results are abnormal, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure, swelling, foamy urine or passing much less urine.
Total calcium measures all the calcium in your blood. Calcium keeps bones strong and helps nerves, muscles and the heart work properly.
Most of your calcium is stored in your bones and teeth.
A small amount in the blood helps muscles contract, nerves send signals and blood clot.
Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D keep blood calcium within a narrow range.
Abnormal calcium can point to problems with the parathyroid glands, vitamin D, kidneys or bones.
Lower calcium is often linked with low albumin, the protein that carries calcium. It can also come from low vitamin D, low magnesium, kidney disease or low parathyroid hormone.
Your calcium is inside the lab's range, suggesting your body is keeping blood calcium well balanced.
Higher calcium is most often caused by an overactive parathyroid gland. Other causes include too much vitamin D or calcium from supplements, dehydration and, less commonly, some cancers.
Your report did not include a reference range for total calcium, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Albumin level: About half of blood calcium travels on albumin, so a low albumin makes total calcium read low even when the active calcium is normal.
Vitamin D: Vitamin D helps your gut absorb calcium; a long shortage can lower it.
Parathyroid hormone: This hormone raises calcium by drawing it from bone and keeping it in the kidneys; an overactive parathyroid gland raises calcium.
Kidney function: Kidneys activate vitamin D and balance calcium, so kidney disease can upset the level.
Calcium or vitamin D supplements: Large doses, especially of vitamin D, can push calcium too high.
Hydration: Dehydration concentrates the blood and can raise calcium a little.
Blood calcium does not show how strong your bones are. The body keeps blood calcium steady by taking it from bone if needed.
Total calcium is affected by albumin. A doctor may correct it for albumin or measure ionised calcium for a truer picture.
Calcium in food, such as milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame and green leafy vegetables, along with enough vitamin D, supports bones.
Include calcium foods such as milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame, or calcium-set tofu. These support bone health.
Getting enough calcium from food and enough vitamin D supports bones, though blood calcium is tightly controlled and rarely changes with diet alone.
See a doctor if calcium is high or low, especially with muscle cramps, tingling, confusion, constipation, extreme thirst or kidney stones.
Chloride is a salt mineral in your blood. It works with sodium to keep the right amount of fluid in your body and the right acid balance in your blood.
Chloride mostly comes from salt in food.
Chloride moves with sodium and water, helping balance fluid inside and outside your cells.
Your kidneys adjust how much chloride leaves in urine.
Chloride is read with sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to check fluid and acid balance.
Lower chloride can happen with long-lasting vomiting, some water tablets (diuretics), heart failure or lung conditions.
Your chloride is inside the lab's range, suggesting normal fluid and salt balance.
Higher chloride often goes with dehydration, or with conditions that make the blood more acidic, such as diarrhoea or some kidney problems.
Your report did not include a reference range for chloride, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Chloride follows water and sodium, so dehydration raises it and too much water lowers it.
Vomiting or diarrhoea: Vomiting loses stomach acid, which contains chloride, so the level falls; severe diarrhoea can raise it.
Kidney function: Healthy kidneys keep this level steady; when filtering falls, the level drifts out of range.
Water tablets (diuretics): Diuretics make the kidneys pass more salt and water and can lower chloride.
Salt intake: Table salt is sodium chloride, though in healthy kidneys the effect on blood chloride is small.
Chloride is rarely a problem on its own. It is read with sodium and bicarbonate to understand fluid and acid balance.
Chloride is rarely meaningful on its own and is interpreted together with sodium and bicarbonate.
Drink water regularly through the day, more in hot weather or after sweating. Good hydration helps your kidneys and keeps results reliable.
Chloride follows salt and fluid balance; dehydration is the most common everyday reason it rises.
See a doctor if chloride is abnormal along with ongoing vomiting, diarrhoea, weakness, confusion or breathing difficulty.
Creatinine is a waste product made by your muscles as they work. Your kidneys filter it out, so its level in blood is a good guide to how well your kidneys are working.
Your muscles make creatinine at a fairly steady rate every day.
Healthy kidneys filter it out of your blood and into your urine.
When kidney filtering slows, creatinine builds up in the blood.
Creatinine is the main blood test for kidney function and is used to calculate eGFR.
Lower creatinine usually reflects less muscle, for example in older or very slim people, or during pregnancy. It is rarely a concern.
Your creatinine is inside the lab's range, suggesting your kidneys are filtering waste normally for your muscle size.
Higher creatinine can mean the kidneys are filtering less well. It can also rise with dehydration, a lot of muscle, eating plenty of meat before the test, creatine supplements or some medicines.
Your report did not include a reference range for creatinine, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Muscle mass: Creatinine comes from normal muscle wear, so people with more muscle make more of it.
Hydration: Being short of water concentrates the blood and slows kidney filtering for a while, so this result can read higher; it settles once you drink normally.
Kidney function: Healthy kidneys keep this level steady; when filtering falls, the level drifts out of range.
Meat eaten before the test: Cooked meat contains creatine, which turns into creatinine, so a large meat meal can raise the level for some hours.
Creatine supplements: Creatine taken for training is turned into creatinine and can make the result read high.
Some medicines: Some medicines stop the kidneys releasing creatinine, raising the level without kidney damage.
A high creatinine in a muscular person or someone taking creatine may not mean kidney damage. Doctors may use other tests to check.
Creatinine depends on muscle size, so the same value can mean different kidney function in different people. eGFR adjusts for some of this.
Keep blood pressure and blood sugar in a healthy range. They are the two most common causes of kidney damage.
Drink water through the day, more in heat or after sweating, and use painkillers such as ibuprofen or diclofenac only as advised.
If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, ask how often your kidneys should be checked. Kidney damage is often silent until late.
Keeping salt low helps blood pressure, which protects the kidney filters.
Drink water regularly through the day, more in hot weather or after sweating. Good hydration helps your kidneys and keeps results reliable.
Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen and diclofenac for long periods without medical advice. They can strain the kidneys.
Keep blood pressure and blood sugar in check with your doctor. These are the two biggest causes of kidney damage.
Dehydration, a large meat meal shortly before the test and creatine supplements can raise creatinine without kidney damage.
Talk to a doctor if kidney results are abnormal, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure, swelling, foamy urine or passing much less urine.
Sodium is the main salt mineral in your blood. It controls how much water your body holds and helps nerves and muscles work.
Sodium mostly comes from salt in food.
Sodium pulls water with it, so it helps decide how much fluid is in your blood and around your cells.
Your kidneys and hormones keep blood sodium within a narrow range.
Abnormal sodium can cause confusion, weakness or seizures, and points to fluid, kidney, hormone or medicine problems.

Lower sodium usually means there is too much water compared with salt. It can come from some medicines such as water tablets, drinking very large amounts of water, heart, liver or kidney conditions, or hormone problems.
Your sodium is inside the lab's range, suggesting your body's water and salt balance is steady.
Higher sodium usually means your body is short of water, for example from not drinking enough, sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea.
Your report did not include a reference range for sodium, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Fluid intake: Drinking far more water than the kidneys can clear dilutes sodium; drinking too little raises it.
Vomiting or diarrhoea: Losing fluid and salt can push sodium either way, depending on what is lost and replaced.
Water tablets and some other medicines: Diuretics and some antidepressants and seizure medicines can lower sodium.

Blood sodium does not show how much salt you eat.
Drink to thirst and a little more in hot weather. Avoid forcing very large amounts of water, which can dilute sodium.
Keep added salt and salty packaged foods low for your blood pressure, even though blood sodium stays steady.
Blood sodium mostly reflects water balance. Eating more salt usually raises blood pressure rather than blood sodium.

Your liver turns waste from protein into urea.
Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys, which filter it into urine.
Urea and BUN measure the same thing in different ways.
Urea helps check kidney function and hydration, usually alongside creatinine.
Lower urea can come from a low-protein diet, drinking a lot of fluid, pregnancy or, less often, liver disease.

Keep blood pressure and blood sugar in a healthy range. They are the two most common causes of kidney damage.
Drink water through the day, more in heat or after sweating, and use painkillers such as ibuprofen or diclofenac only as advised.
Drink water regularly through the day, more in hot weather or after sweating. Good hydration helps your kidneys and keeps results reliable.
Dehydration and high-protein meals can raise urea.

Uric acid is a waste product made when your body breaks down purines, natural substances found in your cells and in some foods.
Purines are found in all body cells and in foods like red meat, organ meat, some seafood and beer.
When purines break down, uric acid forms and is mostly removed by the kidneys.
If too much builds up, it can form sharp crystals in joints or kidneys.
High uric acid can lead to gout, a painful joint condition, and kidney stones. It is also linked with high blood pressure and metabolic health.
Low uric acid is uncommon and usually not a concern.
Your uric acid is inside the lab's range, which lowers the chance of crystals forming in joints or kidneys.

A high uric acid does not mean you have gout, and uric acid can be normal during a gout attack.

The urea to creatinine ratio compares two kidney waste products. It works like the BUN to creatinine ratio, using urea instead of BUN.
Urea changes with hydration and diet, while creatinine is steadier.
The ratio is calculated from your two results.
The ratio helps a doctor think about whether an abnormal kidney result is linked to hydration, diet or the kidneys.
A lower ratio can go with a low-protein diet or liver disease.
Your ratio is inside the lab's range. It matters most when urea or creatinine is abnormal.
A higher ratio often points to dehydration, a high-protein diet or bleeding in the gut.
Your report did not include a reference range for urea to creatinine ratio, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Dehydration raises urea more than creatinine, so the ratio goes up.
Protein intake: A high-protein diet or bleeding in the gut raises urea and the ratio.
Urea level: The top of the ratio; anything that raises urea nitrogen raises the ratio.
Creatinine level: The bottom of the ratio; more muscle or reduced kidney filtering raises creatinine.
The ratio does not measure kidney function by itself. It helps a doctor think about dehydration or bleeding when urea is raised.
The ratio adds little when urea and creatinine are both normal.
Talk to a doctor if urea or creatinine is abnormal.
eGFR estimates how much blood your kidneys clean each minute. The name stands for estimated glomerular (kidney filter) filtration rate.
Each kidney has around a million tiny filters that clean waste and extra water from your blood.
eGFR is calculated from your creatinine, age and sex.
A higher eGFR means your kidneys are filtering more blood. Kidney filtering naturally slows a little with age.
eGFR is the main number used to check for and stage chronic kidney disease, which often has no symptoms early.

A lower eGFR means the kidneys are filtering less blood. A single low result can be caused by dehydration or a large meat meal before the test, so doctors repeat it and check urine before deciding whether it means kidney disease.
Your eGFR is inside the lab's range, suggesting your kidneys are filtering normally for your age.
A higher eGFR usually means the kidneys are filtering well. Very high values are mostly seen in young people or pregnancy and are rarely a concern.
Your report did not include a reference range for estimated kidney filtering rate (eGFR), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Creatinine level: eGFR is calculated from creatinine, so anything that raises creatinine lowers eGFR.
Age: Kidney filtering slowly falls with age, and the formula allows for this.
Muscle mass: Very muscular people can have a falsely low eGFR, and very slim people a falsely high one.
Hydration: Dehydration can lower eGFR for a while.
Diabetes: High blood sugar over years damages the tiny kidney filters.
High blood pressure: Long-term high pressure damages kidney blood vessels and filters.
Lab ranges for eGFR vary. NIDDK notes that an eGFR below 60 may mean kidney disease, whatever the printed range, so a result under 60 is worth discussing with a doctor.
One low eGFR is not a diagnosis. Doctors repeat the test and look at urine results before deciding.
eGFR is an estimate based on creatinine, so it can be less accurate in people with very high or very low muscle mass.
Keep blood pressure and blood sugar in a healthy range. They are the two most common causes of kidney damage.
Drink water through the day, more in heat or after sweating, and use painkillers such as ibuprofen or diclofenac only as advised.
If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, ask how often your kidneys should be checked. Kidney damage is often silent until late.
Keeping salt low helps blood pressure, which protects the kidney filters.
Drink water regularly through the day, more in hot weather or after sweating. Good hydration helps your kidneys and keeps results reliable.
Keep salt low and work with your doctor on blood pressure and blood sugar. These protect the kidney filters.
Avoid long-term use of painkillers like ibuprofen or diclofenac without advice. They can reduce kidney filtering.
Diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes of falling kidney function, so managing them protects eGFR.
Talk to a doctor if eGFR is below the lab's range, has dropped compared with earlier tests, or comes with swelling, foamy urine, or high blood pressure.
Phosphate is a mineral that works with calcium to build bones and teeth. It also helps your cells store and use energy.
Most phosphate is stored in your bones.
The rest helps every cell make energy and build its outer wall.
Your kidneys, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone keep blood phosphate balanced.
Abnormal phosphate can point to kidney disease, vitamin D problems or parathyroid gland problems.
Lower phosphate can come from poor nutrition, heavy alcohol use, an overactive parathyroid gland, low vitamin D or some antacids.
Your phosphate is inside the lab's range, suggesting this mineral is well balanced.
Higher phosphate is most often caused by the kidneys not removing enough. It can also come from low parathyroid hormone or too much vitamin D.
Your report did not include a reference range for phosphate, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Kidney function: Healthy kidneys keep this level steady; when filtering falls, the level drifts out of range.
Vitamin D: Vitamin D helps the gut absorb phosphate.
Parathyroid hormone: This hormone makes the kidneys pass more phosphate, lowering the blood level.
Nutrition: Poor nutrition or refeeding after starvation can lower phosphate.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking can lower phosphate.
Some antacids: Antacids containing aluminium or calcium bind phosphate in the gut and lower it.
Phosphate is rarely about diet alone in healthy people. It mainly reflects kidney and hormone balance.
Phosphate can rise in a sample that was handled slowly, and it varies with recent meals.
Talk to a doctor if phosphate is abnormal, especially with kidney disease, bone pain or muscle weakness.
Potassium is a mineral in your blood that helps your nerves, muscles and especially your heart beat steadily.
Potassium mostly lives inside your cells, with a small amount in the blood.
Potassium helps nerves send signals and muscles, including the heart, contract.
Your kidneys keep blood potassium in a narrow range.
Both high and low potassium can upset the heart's rhythm, so this result is watched closely.
Lower potassium can come from vomiting, diarrhoea, water tablets (diuretics) or not eating enough. It can cause weakness, cramps or an uneven heartbeat.
Your potassium is inside the lab's range, which supports a steady heart rhythm.

Higher potassium can come from kidney problems, some blood pressure medicines or supplements. A falsely high result is common when blood cells burst during sample collection, so a repeat test is often done.
Your report did not include a reference range for potassium, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Kidney function: Healthy kidneys keep this level steady; when filtering falls, the level drifts out of range.
Water tablets and some blood pressure medicines: Some medicines and supplements raise potassium, and water tablets (diuretics) can push it up or down.
Vomiting or diarrhoea: Fluid loss from the gut can lower potassium.
Sample handling: Clenching your fist hard during the blood draw can raise potassium for a while and give an incorrect result.
Potassium supplements: Supplements or salt substitutes can raise it, especially with kidney problems.
A single high potassium is often a sample problem, but it is still repeated quickly because a truly high level can affect the heart.
A falsely high potassium is common if the blood sample was difficult to take or delayed, so an unexpected high value is usually repeated.
Eat a variety of fruits and vegetables each day. They provide potassium, which also helps balance the effect of salt on blood pressure.
Fruits and vegetables like banana, coconut water, potato, tomato and leafy greens are good sources of potassium.
Seek medical care promptly if potassium is clearly high or low, or you have palpitations, chest discomfort, muscle weakness or cramps.
If you have kidney disease, check with your doctor before eating more potassium-rich foods or salt substitutes.
Magnesium is a mineral your body uses for hundreds of processes, including muscle and nerve work, energy production and keeping a steady heartbeat.
Most magnesium is stored in your bones and inside cells. Only a small amount is in the blood.
Magnesium helps muscles relax after they contract and helps nerves send signals.
Your kidneys control how much magnesium your body keeps.
Low magnesium can cause cramps, tiredness and heart rhythm problems, and it can make low calcium and low potassium harder to correct.
Lower magnesium can come from a diet low in whole foods, heavy alcohol use, diarrhoea, diabetes, or medicines such as water tablets and long-term acid-reducing tablets.
Your blood magnesium is inside the lab's range, although blood levels do not always show how much is stored in the body.
Higher magnesium is uncommon. It is usually linked with kidney problems or taking magnesium in antacids, laxatives or supplements.
Your report did not include a reference range for magnesium, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Diet: Whole grains, dal, nuts, seeds and green vegetables supply magnesium; diets low in these can be low in it.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking makes the kidneys pass more magnesium.
Diarrhoea: Long-lasting diarrhoea loses magnesium from the gut.
Diabetes: Poorly controlled diabetes makes the kidneys pass more magnesium.
Water tablets or acid-reducing medicines: Some diuretics and long-term acid-reducing tablets lower magnesium.
Kidney function: Kidney disease can raise magnesium, especially with magnesium-containing antacids.
Blood magnesium can look normal even when body stores are a little low, because most magnesium sits inside cells and bone.
Blood magnesium can be normal even when the body's stores are low.
Whole grains, dal, nuts and seeds, and green leafy vegetables are everyday sources of magnesium.
Include magnesium-rich foods such as nuts, seeds, whole grains, dal and leafy greens. Food is the safest way to keep magnesium topped up.
Keep alcohol low. Alcohol makes the kidneys lose magnesium.
Whole grains, nuts, seeds, pulses and leafy green vegetables are good sources of magnesium.
Talk to a doctor if magnesium is abnormal, especially with muscle cramps, twitching, an irregular heartbeat or kidney disease. Do not take magnesium supplements with kidney disease unless advised.
Zinc is a trace mineral your body needs in small amounts for immunity, wound healing, taste and smell, and growth.
Zinc helps your immune cells fight infection.
Zinc is needed to heal wounds and to make new cells and proteins.
Your body cannot store much zinc, so you need some from food regularly.
Low zinc can weaken immunity, slow healing and affect taste, skin and hair.
Lower zinc can come from a diet low in zinc foods, poor absorption from the gut, diarrhoea, heavy alcohol use or ongoing illness. Inflammation can also lower blood zinc temporarily.
Your zinc is inside the lab's range, suggesting you are getting enough for now.
Higher zinc is uncommon and usually comes from taking zinc supplements. Too much zinc over time can lower copper levels.
Your report did not include a reference range for zinc, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Diet: Zinc comes from dal, nuts, seeds, whole grains, dairy, eggs and meat; phytates, natural compounds in some grains and pulses, reduce how much is absorbed.
Gut absorption: Gut conditions can reduce absorption.
Inflammation or illness: During illness zinc moves out of the blood into tissues, so the blood level falls without a true shortage.
Alcohol: Alcohol reduces absorption and increases loss.
Zinc supplements: Supplements raise the level; very high doses can lower copper.
Time of day the sample was taken: Zinc is highest in the morning and falls after meals.
A low zinc during an illness may not mean you need supplements. The level often recovers once the illness settles.
Blood zinc falls during infection and inflammation and changes with time of day, so it does not always reflect body stores.
A varied diet with dal, nuts, seeds and whole grains supplies zinc for most people.
Include zinc foods such as pumpkin seeds, chana, rajma, nuts, curd, eggs or meat. Regular intake matters because the body stores little zinc.
If you are vegetarian, soak, sprout or ferment pulses and grains. This helps your body absorb more zinc from them.
Meat, eggs, seafood, dairy, pulses, nuts, seeds and whole grains provide zinc.
Zinc from plant foods is absorbed less well, so vegetarians may need a little more.
Talk to a doctor if zinc is low with slow wound healing, frequent infections, hair loss or changes in taste, or if you take zinc supplements regularly.
Vitamin B12 is a vitamin your body needs to make healthy red blood cells, keep nerves working and make DNA, the genetic material in your cells.
B12 comes naturally from animal foods such as milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish and meat. Fortified foods, such as some breakfast cereals and plant milks, also supply it.
Your stomach needs acid and a protein called intrinsic factor to absorb B12.
Your liver stores B12, so a shortage can take months or years to show.
Low B12 can cause tiredness, anaemia, tingling, numbness and memory problems. Nerve damage can become permanent if a shortage lasts a long time.
