Lower B12 often comes from eating few animal foods, as in vegetarian and vegan diets. Poor absorption in the stomach or gut, and medicines such as metformin or long-term acid-reducing tablets, can also lower it, so people who eat meat can be low too. A low B12 is one possible reason for large red cells or anaemia, but other causes need checking too.
Your vitamin B12 is inside the lab's range. Some people with results near the lower end can still have a mild shortage, so symptoms matter.

Higher B12 is usually from supplements, injections or fortified foods and is not known to be harmful. A high level without supplements is uncommon and can sometimes go with liver, kidney or blood conditions, so it is worth mentioning to a doctor.
Your report did not include a reference range for vitamin B12, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Vegetarian or vegan diet: B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods, so diets with little or no dairy, eggs, fish or meat supply less.
Stomach or gut absorption: B12 needs stomach acid and a protein called intrinsic factor to be absorbed; some stomach and gut conditions, including pernicious anaemia, block this.
Metformin: This diabetes medicine can lower B12 absorption over years.
Long-term acid-reducing tablets: Less stomach acid means less B12 is freed from food.
Age: Absorption falls with age, even when the diet contains enough.
Supplements: B12 tablets or injections raise the level, often above the printed range, which is generally not harmful.
Eating dairy every day does not guarantee enough B12. Absorption problems can cause a shortage whatever you eat.
A B12 shortage is not the only reason red cells become large. Folate, alcohol, thyroid and liver problems can do it too, so a doctor checks the cause.
Blood B12 does not always reflect how much B12 your cells can use, so borderline results are sometimes checked with other tests.
Dairy and eggs every day, if you eat them, or fortified foods if you are vegan, keep B12 supply steady.
If you take metformin or long-term acid-reducing tablets, ask whether your B12 should be checked regularly.
Include milk, curd, paneer or eggs daily if you eat them. They are the main vegetarian sources of B12.
If you are vegan, look for foods fortified with B12, such as some plant milks and cereals. Plant foods do not naturally contain it.
B12 is found naturally only in animal foods, so vegetarians and vegans are at higher risk of low levels.
Absorption falls with age and with some stomach conditions, even when the diet contains enough.
Talk to a doctor if B12 is low, especially with tingling, numbness, balance problems, memory changes or anaemia. They can find the cause and advise on treatment.
This test measures 25-hydroxy vitamin D, the main form of vitamin D stored in your blood. It is the best guide to your vitamin D levels.
Your skin makes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight. Some also comes from food.
Your liver turns it into 25-hydroxy vitamin D, the form this test measures.
Vitamin D helps your gut absorb calcium for strong bones and also supports muscles and immunity.
Low vitamin D is very common and can lead to weak bones, bone pain and muscle weakness.

Lower vitamin D is often due to little time in sunlight, covering most skin, darker skin, staying indoors, extra body weight, or few vitamin D foods. Some gut, liver and kidney conditions also lower it.
Your vitamin D is inside the lab's range, which supports healthy bones and muscles.
Higher vitamin D is almost always caused by taking too much from supplements. NIH describes levels above 50 ng/mL as too high; very large doses can cause nausea, kidney stones and kidney damage.
Your report did not include a reference range for vitamin D (25-hydroxy), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Sunlight exposure: Skin makes vitamin D in sunlight; working indoors, covering most skin and pollution reduce this.
Skin colour: Darker skin makes vitamin D more slowly from the same sunlight.
Body weight: Vitamin D is stored in body fat, so people with more body fat tend to have lower blood levels.
Diet: Few Indian foods are rich in vitamin D; eggs, oily fish and fortified milk or cereals help a little.
Supplements: Tablets or sachets raise the level; very large doses for a long time can push it too high.
Gut, liver or kidney conditions: The gut absorbs vitamin D and the liver and kidneys activate it, so conditions of these organs lower it.

NIH describes 20 ng/mL or above as adequate for most people and below 12 ng/mL as too low. Many labs print a higher lower limit, such as 30 ng/mL, so a result between 20 and 30 may be flagged low; a doctor decides whether treatment is needed.
Living in a sunny country does not prevent low vitamin D. Low levels are very common in India.
More is not better. NIH describes levels above 50 ng/mL as too high, and very large doses can cause nausea, kidney stones and kidney damage.
Labs use different methods and cut-offs for vitamin D, so the same number may be labelled differently by different labs.
Some regular daylight on uncovered arms and face, when safe for your skin, plus vitamin D foods that suit your diet, help keep levels up.
Spend some time outdoors in daylight with arms and face uncovered, when safe for your skin. Sunlight helps your skin make vitamin D.
Include vitamin D foods such as eggs, oily fish or fortified milk and cereals if they suit your diet.
Stay physically active with walking or strength exercise. This supports bones and muscles alongside vitamin D.
Sunlight on the skin is the main natural source of vitamin D.
Few foods contain much vitamin D. Oily fish, egg yolks and fortified milk or cereals are the main ones.
Talk to a doctor if vitamin D is low, especially with bone pain or muscle weakness, or if you take high-dose supplements and your level is high. They will advise on any treatment and dose.
Vitamin C is a vitamin your body uses to heal wounds, build healthy skin and blood vessels, and absorb iron from plant foods.
Your body cannot make or store much vitamin C, so it needs a regular supply from food.
Vitamin C helps make collagen, a protein that holds skin, gums and blood vessels together.
Vitamin C also protects cells from damage and helps you absorb iron.
Low vitamin C can cause tiredness, bleeding gums, slow wound healing and poor iron absorption.
Lower vitamin C usually means you are not eating enough fruit and vegetables. Smoking, heavy alcohol use and some illnesses also lower it.
Your vitamin C is inside the lab's range, suggesting you are getting enough from your diet.
Higher vitamin C usually comes from supplements. Very large doses can upset the stomach and may raise the chance of kidney stones in some people.
Your report did not include a reference range for vitamin C, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Fruit and vegetable intake: Vitamin C comes from fruit and vegetables such as amla, guava, citrus and capsicum; the body cannot store much.
Smoking: Smoking uses up vitamin C faster, so smokers need more.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking lowers intake and absorption.
Illness or inflammation: Illness lowers the blood level as the body uses more.
Supplements: Tablets raise the level for some hours.
Recent meals: A vitamin C-rich meal shortly before the test can raise the result.
Vitamin C supplements have not been shown to prevent colds in most people.
Blood vitamin C reflects recent intake more than long-term stores.
Fresh fruit and vegetables every day, such as amla, guava, oranges and capsicum, keep vitamin C topped up. Cooking for a long time destroys some of it.
Eat at least one fresh fruit or raw vegetable each day, such as amla, guava, orange or tomato. Your body needs a daily supply.
Pair vitamin C foods with iron-rich meals, such as lemon on dal or spinach. This helps you absorb more iron.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Smoking uses up vitamin C faster.
Citrus fruits, amla, guava, kiwi, tomatoes, capsicum and leafy greens are rich in vitamin C. Long cooking destroys some of it.
Talk to a doctor if vitamin C is low with bleeding gums, easy bruising or slow healing.
T3 is one of the two main thyroid hormones. It is the active form that tells your cells how fast to use energy.
Your thyroid gland in the neck makes mostly T4 and a smaller amount of T3.
Much of the T3 in your body is made by converting T4 in other tissues.
T3 affects heart rate, body temperature, digestion and energy levels.
T3 helps confirm and judge the severity of an overactive thyroid, and is read with TSH and T4.
Lower T3 can be seen with an underactive thyroid, but it also often falls during illness, fasting or stress even when the thyroid is healthy.
Your T3 is inside the lab's range. It is read together with TSH and T4.
Higher T3 usually points to an overactive thyroid. It can also rise in pregnancy or with some hormone medicines.
Your report did not include a reference range for T3 thyroid hormone, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Thyroid gland activity: An overactive gland makes more thyroid hormone and an underactive one makes less, often from autoimmune thyroid disease.
Illness or fasting: During serious illness or fasting the body makes less active T3 to save energy, without a thyroid problem.
Pregnancy: Pregnancy hormones raise the proteins that carry thyroid hormone, which changes total T3.
Some medicines: Steroids, beta blockers and some heart medicines can change T3.
T3 is not usually the first test for thyroid problems. TSH is, and T3 helps mainly when an overactive thyroid is suspected.
T3 is not a good test on its own for an underactive thyroid, because it often stays normal or falls for other reasons.
If you take thyroid tablets, take them the same way every day, usually on an empty stomach, and have levels checked as advised.
Talk to a doctor if your thyroid results are abnormal, especially with tiredness, weight change, feeling unusually hot or cold, a racing heart, or changes in periods or mood.
T4 is the main hormone made by your thyroid gland. Your body turns it into T3, the active form that controls how fast your cells use energy.
Your thyroid makes T4 when it receives a signal called TSH from the brain.
T4 travels in the blood and is converted into T3 in tissues like the liver.
Together, these hormones set your body's pace, affecting energy, weight, temperature and heart rate.
T4 is used with TSH to check whether the thyroid is underactive or overactive.
Lower T4 usually points to an underactive thyroid. Less often, it comes from a problem with the brain signal that controls the thyroid.
Your T4 is inside the lab's range, suggesting your thyroid is making enough of its main hormone.
Higher T4 usually points to an overactive thyroid. It can also rise in pregnancy, with some medicines, or if thyroid tablets are at too high a dose.
Your report did not include a reference range for T4 thyroid hormone, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Thyroid gland activity: An overactive gland makes more thyroid hormone and an underactive one makes less, often from autoimmune thyroid disease.
Pregnancy: Pregnancy raises the proteins that carry T4, which changes total T4.
Thyroid tablets: Levothyroxine is T4, so the dose and timing of the last tablet affect the result.

Some medicines and supplements such as biotin: High-dose biotin, common in hair, skin and nail supplements, can interfere with many thyroid tests and give falsely high or low results, so tell the lab or doctor if you take it.
Thyroid problems are not only about weight. Tiredness, feeling cold or hot, periods, mood and heart rate can all change.
Biotin supplements can interfere with some thyroid tests. Tell your doctor if you take biotin.
If you take thyroid tablets, take them the same way every day, usually on an empty stomach, and have levels checked as advised.
Talk to a doctor if your thyroid results are abnormal, especially with tiredness, weight change, feeling unusually hot or cold, a racing heart, or changes in periods or mood.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, is a signal from your brain that tells your thyroid gland how much hormone to make. It is the main first test of thyroid health.
The pituitary gland in your brain watches your thyroid hormone levels.
If thyroid hormones are low, it sends out more TSH to push the thyroid to work harder.
If thyroid hormones are high, TSH drops. So TSH moves in the opposite direction to thyroid hormones.
TSH is usually the first test to check for an underactive or overactive thyroid, and to adjust thyroid treatment.
A lower TSH usually means the thyroid is overactive, or thyroid tablets are at too high a dose. Less often, it comes from a problem with the pituitary gland.
Your TSH is inside the lab's range, which usually means your thyroid is working normally.

A higher TSH usually means the thyroid is underactive, so the brain is pushing harder. Common causes include autoimmune thyroid disease and thyroid tablets at too low a dose. Mild rises can be temporary, for example after an illness.
Your report did not include a reference range for thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Thyroid gland activity: TSH comes from the pituitary gland in the brain. When the thyroid is underactive, TSH rises to push it; when overactive, TSH falls.
Thyroid tablets: Too low a dose leaves TSH high and too high a dose pushes it low.
Recent illness: TSH can be briefly high or low during and after an illness.
Pregnancy: TSH is often a little low during the first three months of pregnancy, so results in pregnancy are judged differently.
Some medicines: Steroids, some heart medicines and others can change TSH.
Biotin supplements: Biotin can interfere with the lab test and give misleading results.

TSH ranges differ between labs, and TSH is often a little low in the first three months of pregnancy, so a result just outside the printed range is judged with your symptoms, your T4 and whether you are pregnant.
A slightly high TSH does not always need tablets. Mild rises are often rechecked, especially after an illness.
A single mildly abnormal TSH is often repeated, as illness, timing and some medicines can shift it.
If you take thyroid tablets, take them the same way every day, usually on an empty stomach, and have levels checked as advised.
If you take thyroid tablets, take them the same way every day, usually on an empty stomach. Consistency keeps your levels steady.
Iodine in food, such as iodised salt, is needed to make thyroid hormones. Most people using iodised salt get enough.
Talk to a doctor if your thyroid results are abnormal, especially with tiredness, weight change, feeling unusually hot or cold, a racing heart, or changes in periods or mood.
Ask about thyroid testing before or early in pregnancy, as thyroid levels matter for the baby.
Basophils are a type of white blood cell. They are the least common type and are involved in allergic reactions and inflammation.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Basophils are the rarest white cell. They release histamine and other chemicals during allergic reactions and inflammation.
This count shows how many of these cells are in a set amount of blood.
Basophils are rarely important alone; a persistently raised count can sometimes point to allergy or a bone marrow condition.
A lower basophil count is common and usually not a concern, as basophils are normally very few.
Your basophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher basophil count can be seen with allergies, ongoing inflammation, an underactive thyroid or, rarely, some bone marrow conditions.
Your report did not include a reference range for basophil count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Allergy: Allergic reactions can raise basophils slightly.
Ongoing inflammation: Long-term inflammation can raise them.
Underactive thyroid: An underactive thyroid is sometimes linked with higher basophils.
Bone marrow conditions: A persistently high count can rarely come from the bone marrow.
A low basophil count is not a problem. They are normally so few that zero is a common result.
One result can change with a recent infection or stress, so a single mild change is often rechecked.
Talk to a doctor if your basophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell. They help fight parasites and take part in allergic reactions such as asthma and hay fever.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Eosinophils fight parasites, such as worms, and take part in allergic reactions such as asthma, hay fever and eczema.
This count shows how many of these cells are in a set amount of blood.
Eosinophils help point to allergy or a parasite infection when they are raised.
A lower eosinophil count is usually not a concern. It can fall with stress, steroid medicines or the body's response to infection.
Your eosinophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher eosinophil count is most often caused by allergies, asthma, eczema or parasite infections. Some medicines can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for eosinophil count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Allergy, asthma or eczema: Allergic reactions call eosinophils into the blood and tissues.
Parasite infections: Worm infections, common in India, strongly raise eosinophils.
Some medicines: Some medicines cause an allergic-type reaction that raises eosinophils.
Steroid medicines and acute stress: Steroids and stress hormones lower eosinophils.
High eosinophils are not always allergy. Worm infections are a common cause in India, so a doctor may check stool or treat for worms.
One result can change with a recent infection or stress, so a single mild change is often rechecked.
Talk to a doctor if your eosinophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell. They include cells that make antibodies and cells that fight viruses.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Lymphocytes include the cells that make antibodies and the cells that kill virus-infected cells. They also remember past infections.
This count shows how many of these cells are in a set amount of blood.
Lymphocytes help show a recent viral infection and, when low, how well the immune system can respond.
A lower lymphocyte count can happen during acute illness, stress, with steroid medicines, or with conditions that weaken immunity.
Your lymphocytes result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher lymphocyte count is often seen during or after a viral infection. Less often, it can be due to a long-lasting infection or a blood condition.
Your report did not include a reference range for lymphocyte count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Viral infections: Lymphocytes multiply to fight viruses, so the count rises during and after a viral illness.
Long-lasting infections: Infections such as tuberculosis can raise lymphocytes.
Acute illness and stress: Severe illness and stress hormones lower lymphocytes for a while.
Steroid medicines: Steroids lower the lymphocyte count.
Conditions that weaken immunity: Some infections, such as HIV, and some treatments reduce lymphocytes.
Blood conditions: Less often, a raised count comes from a blood condition, especially in older adults.
A raised lymphocyte count after a cold or fever is usually the immune system doing its job.
One result can change with a recent infection or stress, so a single mild change is often rechecked.
Talk to a doctor if your lymphocytes result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
Monocytes are a type of white blood cell. They clean up germs and damaged cells and help with healing.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Monocytes travel to tissues, where they become clean-up cells that swallow germs and dead cells and help healing.
This count shows how many of these cells are in a set amount of blood.
Monocytes help show recovery from infection or a long-lasting infection or inflammation.
A lower monocyte count is usually not a concern on its own. It can be seen with steroid medicines or some bone marrow problems.
Your monocytes result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher monocyte count can be seen while recovering from infection, with ongoing infections or inflammation, or, less often, with some blood conditions.
Your report did not include a reference range for monocyte count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Recovery from infection: Monocytes often rise as the body clears an infection.
Long-lasting infections: Infections such as tuberculosis raise monocytes.
Inflammatory conditions: Ongoing inflammation, such as inflammatory bowel disease, raises them.
Steroid medicines: Steroids lower monocytes.
Bone marrow conditions: Less often, a persistent change comes from the bone marrow.
A mildly high monocyte count after an infection is common and often settles on its own.
One result can change with a recent infection or stress, so a single mild change is often rechecked.
Talk to a doctor if your monocytes result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
Neutrophils are a type of white blood cell. They are the most common type and the first responders to bacterial infections.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Neutrophils are the most common white cell. They are the first to arrive at a bacterial infection or injury and swallow germs.
This count shows how many of these cells are in a set amount of blood.
Neutrophils help show whether the body is fighting a bacterial infection or physical stress, and a low count shows how well protected you are against infection.

A lower neutrophil count can come from viral infections, some medicines, low B12 or folate, or bone marrow problems. It can also be naturally lower in some healthy people, including many people of African, Middle Eastern or South Asian descent.
Your neutrophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher neutrophil count is most often caused by a bacterial infection, inflammation, injury, physical stress, smoking or steroid medicines.
Your report did not include a reference range for neutrophil count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Bacterial infection: The marrow releases extra neutrophils to fight bacteria, so the count rises.
Physical stress, injury or surgery: Stress hormones push neutrophils from the vessel walls into the bloodstream.
Smoking: Smoking keeps the body in a low-grade inflamed state, raising neutrophils.
Steroid medicines: Steroids raise the neutrophil count.
Viral infections: Some viral infections, including dengue, temporarily lower neutrophils.
Some medicines: Some antibiotics, thyroid medicines and cancer treatments can lower neutrophils.
Low B12 or folate: The marrow needs these vitamins to make all blood cells.
Inherited lower counts: Many healthy people of South Asian, African or Middle Eastern descent naturally have lower neutrophils without extra infections.
A slightly low neutrophil count in a well person is often a normal variation, especially in people of South Asian descent, but it is still worth a doctor's view if it persists.
One result can change with a recent infection or stress, so a single mild change is often rechecked.
Talk to a doctor if your neutrophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
The erythrocyte (red blood cell) sedimentation rate, or ESR, measures how quickly red blood cells settle to the bottom of a tube. Faster settling is a general sign of inflammation.
During inflammation, the liver releases proteins that make red cells clump together.
Clumped cells are heavier and settle faster.
So ESR shows that inflammation may be present, but not where or why.
ESR is a simple check for inflammation and is used to follow some long-term inflammatory conditions.
A lower ESR is usually not a concern. Some conditions lower it, such as having too many red cells (polycythaemia), sickle cell anaemia or heart failure.
Your ESR is inside the lab's range, suggesting no marked inflammation from this test.

A higher ESR can come from infection, inflammation, autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, anaemia, pregnancy, kidney disease or thyroid disease. The normal upper limit is higher in older adults and in women.
Your report did not include a reference range for red cell settling rate (automated ESR), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Infection: Infection makes the liver release proteins that cause red cells to clump, so they settle faster.
Inflammation: Any inflammation raises these proteins and the ESR.
Age and sex: The normal upper limit is higher in older adults and in women.
Anaemia: With fewer red cells in the tube, the cells settle faster, raising ESR without inflammation.
Pregnancy: Pregnancy raises ESR.
Autoimmune conditions: Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus raise ESR.
Kidney disease: Kidney disease can raise ESR.
Thyroid disease: Thyroid disease can raise ESR.
Red cell and heart conditions: Too many red cells (polycythaemia), sickle cell anaemia and heart failure lower ESR.
A normal ESR does not rule out inflammation, and a raised ESR does not show where it is. CRP is often checked alongside it.
ESR is non-specific. A normal ESR does not rule out inflammation, and a raised ESR does not show the cause.
Talk to a doctor if ESR is high, especially with unexplained fever, joint pain, muscle symptoms or a new headache.
Haemoglobin is the protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. It also gives blood its red colour.
Each red blood cell is packed with haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it in your tissues.
Your body needs iron, vitamin B12 and folate to make haemoglobin.
Low haemoglobin, called anaemia, is very common and can cause tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin.
Lower haemoglobin means anaemia. Common causes include low iron, often from heavy periods or a diet low in iron, low vitamin B12 or folate, blood loss and long-term illness.
Your haemoglobin is inside the lab's range, suggesting your blood is carrying oxygen well.
Higher haemoglobin can come from dehydration, smoking, living at high altitude or lung conditions. Less often, the bone marrow makes too many red cells.
Your report did not include a reference range for haemoglobin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron, B12 and folate levels: The marrow needs iron to build haemoglobin and B12 and folate to make red cells; a shortage of any lowers it.
Blood loss including heavy periods: Losing blood, often slowly through heavy periods or the gut, uses up iron and lowers haemoglobin.
Inherited haemoglobin traits: Thalassaemia trait, common in India, can give a mildly low haemoglobin with small red cells, unrelated to iron.
Long-term illness: Kidney disease and ongoing inflammation slow red cell production.
Hydration: Dehydration concentrates the blood and makes haemoglobin read higher.
Smoking: Carbon monoxide from smoke reduces oxygen delivery, so the body makes more haemoglobin.
Altitude: Living high up, where air has less oxygen, raises haemoglobin.
Not every low haemoglobin is from low iron. Thalassaemia trait, B12 or folate shortage and long-term illness can cause it, so iron tablets should not be started without finding the cause.
Haemoglobin shows whether anaemia is present, but not its cause. Red cell indices and iron or vitamin tests help with that.
Iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, eggs, fish or meat, eaten with a vitamin C food such as lemon, amla or guava, help keep iron stores up.
Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption, so having them an hour away from meals helps.
Heavy periods are the most common reason Indian women run low on iron. If periods are heavy, tell your doctor.
Include iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, jaggery in moderation, eggs, fish or meat. Your body needs iron to make haemoglobin.
Have a vitamin C food with iron-rich meals, such as lemon, amla, guava or tomato. Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods.
Keep tea and coffee away from meals by about an hour. They reduce how much iron you absorb.
Iron-rich foods, with vitamin C to help absorption, support healthy haemoglobin. Vegetarians may need to plan iron sources more carefully.
Talk to a doctor if haemoglobin is low, so they can find the cause before treatment. Do not start iron tablets without checking first.
Seek care promptly if low haemoglobin comes with chest pain, fainting, black stools or heavy bleeding.
MCH, or mean corpuscular haemoglobin, shows the average amount of haemoglobin inside each red blood cell.
Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells.
MCH tells you how much of it, on average, each cell contains.
MCH helps work out the type and likely cause of anaemia.
A lower MCH means red cells contain less haemoglobin than usual. The most common cause is low iron. Inherited conditions such as thalassaemia trait can also cause it.
Your MCH is inside the lab's range, suggesting your red cells carry a normal amount of haemoglobin.
A higher MCH usually means red cells are larger than usual, which can happen with low vitamin B12 or folate, liver disease or heavy alcohol use.
Your report did not include a reference range for haemoglobin per red blood cell (MCH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: Low iron means less haemoglobin is packed into each cell, lowering MCH.
Vitamin B12 and folate: Shortages make cells larger, each carrying more haemoglobin, raising MCH.
Thalassaemia trait: This inherited trait gives small cells with less haemoglobin each.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking can enlarge red cells and raise MCH.
MCH rarely needs separate action. It follows MCV and is read with it.
MCH is read together with MCV and haemoglobin; on its own it cannot diagnose a cause.
Low iron intake is the most common everyday reason MCH falls.
Talk to a doctor if MCH is abnormal together with low haemoglobin, to find the cause.
MCHC, or mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration, shows how concentrated the haemoglobin is inside your red blood cells.
MCHC compares the amount of haemoglobin with the size of the red cells.
MCHC helps describe how well each cell is filled with haemoglobin.
MCHC helps describe the type of anaemia and can point to some inherited red cell conditions.
A lower MCHC means red cells are paler than usual, most often because of low iron.
Your MCHC is inside the lab's range.
A higher MCHC is uncommon. It can be seen with some inherited red cell shape conditions or when red cells are breaking down. Sample problems can also cause it.
Your report did not include a reference range for haemoglobin concentration in red cells (MCHC), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: Long-term low iron makes cells paler, lowering MCHC.
Inherited red cell conditions: Conditions such as hereditary spherocytosis raise MCHC.
Sample handling: A sample with fatty blood or clumped cells can give a falsely high result.
A slightly unusual MCHC with otherwise normal results is often a lab variation.
MCHC changes less than other red cell measures, so it is mainly useful alongside MCV and MCH.
Talk to a doctor if MCHC is abnormal together with other red cell changes.
MCV, or mean corpuscular volume, shows the average size of your red blood cells.
Red cells are normally a fairly even size.
Low iron tends to make them smaller, while low B12 or folate tends to make them larger.
MCV is one of the most useful clues to the cause of anaemia.
A lower MCV means red cells are smaller than usual. The most common cause is low iron. Thalassaemia trait, an inherited condition, is another common cause.
Your MCV is inside the lab's range, suggesting your red cells are a normal size.
A higher MCV means red cells are larger than usual. Common causes are low vitamin B12 or folate, heavy alcohol use, liver disease, an underactive thyroid and some medicines.
Your report did not include a reference range for average red blood cell size (MCV), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: Without enough iron, cells are made smaller.
Vitamin B12 and folate: Without these, cells cannot divide properly and stay large.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking enlarges red cells.
Thalassaemia trait: This common inherited trait makes cells small, without low iron.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid can enlarge red cells.
Liver disease and some medicines: Liver disease and some medicines, such as some used for seizures or HIV, enlarge red cells.
Small red cells do not always mean low iron. Thalassaemia trait is common in India and needs different advice.
Low iron and low B12 together can cancel out, giving a normal MCV even when both are low.
Low iron intake makes cells smaller, while low B12 intake, common in vegetarian diets, can make them larger.
Talk to a doctor if MCV is abnormal, especially with low haemoglobin or tiredness, so the cause can be found.
MPV, or mean platelet volume, shows the average size of your platelets. Platelets are tiny blood cells that help your blood clot.
Platelets are made in the bone marrow.
Young platelets are usually larger, so MPV can hint at how quickly new platelets are being made.
MPV helps explain why a platelet count is high or low.
A lower MPV can be seen when the bone marrow is making fewer platelets.
Your MPV is inside the lab's range.
A higher MPV can mean the bone marrow is making many new platelets, for example after platelets have been used up or destroyed.
Your report did not include a reference range for average platelet size (MPV), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Platelet production: When the marrow makes platelets quickly, as after bleeding, new platelets are larger.
Platelet destruction: When platelets are used up quickly, the young large ones dominate.
Sample timing and handling: Platelets swell in the tube over time, so delays raise MPV.
MPV on its own is rarely meaningful. It helps a doctor read an abnormal platelet count.
MPV is affected by how long the sample sits before testing, and it is not useful on its own.
Talk to a doctor if MPV is abnormal together with an abnormal platelet count, or with easy bruising or bleeding.
Haematocrit, also called PCV, shows what share of your blood is made up of red blood cells.
Blood is made of red cells, white cells, platelets and a liquid called plasma.
Haematocrit is the percentage taken up by red cells.
Haematocrit helps confirm anaemia and shows whether you may be dehydrated or have too many red cells.
A lower haematocrit usually goes with anaemia, from causes such as low iron, low B12 or folate, or blood loss.
Your haematocrit is inside the lab's range.
A higher haematocrit can come from dehydration, smoking, high altitude or lung conditions. Less often, the bone marrow makes too many red cells.
Your report did not include a reference range for red blood cell share (haematocrit), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Dehydration reduces the fluid part of blood, raising haematocrit.
Haemoglobin and iron levels: Haematocrit falls with anaemia from low iron or other causes.
Smoking: Smoking raises red cell mass.
Altitude: Living high up raises red cells.
Haematocrit tells the same story as haemoglobin in most people, so they are read together.
Haematocrit usually moves with haemoglobin and adds little on its own.
Dehydration raises haematocrit; low iron intake can lower it through anaemia.
Talk to a doctor if haematocrit is abnormal along with abnormal haemoglobin.
Platelets are tiny blood cells that help stop bleeding by forming clots. The platelet count shows how many you have.
Platelets are made in the bone marrow and live for about a week to ten days.
When a blood vessel is damaged, they stick together to plug the gap.
Too few platelets can lead to easy bleeding, and too many can raise the chance of clots.

A lower platelet count can follow viral infections such as dengue, or come from some medicines, heavy alcohol use, an enlarged spleen, low B12 or folate, or immune conditions. Clumping in the sample tube can also give a falsely low result.
Your platelet count is inside the lab's range, suggesting normal clotting cells.
A higher platelet count is most often a reaction to infection, inflammation, low iron or recent bleeding or surgery. Less often, the bone marrow makes too many.
Your report did not include a reference range for platelet count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Infection: Many infections raise platelets as part of the body's reaction, while viral infections such as dengue lower them.
Inflammation: Ongoing inflammation raises platelets.
Low iron: Iron shortage often raises platelets.
Some medicines: Some antibiotics, heparin and others can lower platelets.
Alcohol: Heavy drinking lowers platelets.
Sample clumping: Platelets can clump in the tube and give a falsely low count.
Papaya leaf juice is not a proven treatment for low platelets in dengue. Dengue needs medical monitoring.
A low count can be falsely low if platelets clumped in the tube, so an unexpected low result is often repeated.
Heavy alcohol use can lower platelets.
Seek care promptly if platelets are low with bleeding gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stools, or many small red or purple spots on the skin.
Talk to a doctor if platelets stay high or low on repeat tests.
The white blood cell count, or WBC, shows how many infection-fighting cells are in your blood.
White blood cells are part of your immune system.
Your body sends more of them into the blood when fighting infection or inflammation.
There are five main types, shown separately in your report.
WBC helps spot infection, inflammation and, less often, bone marrow or immune problems.
A lower WBC can follow viral infections, or come from some medicines, low B12 or folate, autoimmune conditions or bone marrow problems. Some healthy people naturally run lower.
Your white cell count is inside the lab's range.
A higher WBC is most often caused by an infection or inflammation. Stress, smoking, pregnancy and steroid medicines can also raise it. Less often, it is due to a blood condition.
Your report did not include a reference range for white blood cell count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Infection: Bacterial infections usually raise the count; some viral infections lower it.
Inflammation: Ongoing inflammation raises white cells.
Stress: Physical stress and hard exercise push white cells into the blood for a while.
Smoking: Smoking keeps white cells slightly raised.
Some medicines: Steroids raise the count; some antibiotics, thyroid medicines and cancer treatments lower it.
Bone marrow conditions: Less often, a persistently abnormal count comes from the marrow.
A slightly high white count during a cold is normal and usually settles.
The total count does not show which white cell type has changed. The separate counts help with that.
Smoking can raise the white cell count.
Talk to a doctor if WBC is clearly high or low, or comes with fever, frequent infections, weight loss or night sweats.
RDW, or red cell distribution width, shows how much your red blood cells vary in size.
Healthy red cells are mostly a similar size.
When new cells are made under strain, for example with low iron or B12, sizes become more mixed.
A high RDW can be an early clue to low iron or low B12, sometimes before haemoglobin falls.
A low RDW is not a concern.
Your RDW is inside the lab's range, suggesting your red cells are a fairly even size.
A higher RDW means red cells are more mixed in size. It is commonly seen with low iron, low B12 or folate, or recovery from blood loss.
Your report did not include a reference range for red cell size variation (RDW), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: As iron runs low, new cells are smaller than old ones, so sizes vary more.
Vitamin B12 and folate: Shortages produce larger cells alongside normal ones.
Recent blood loss or treatment: After bleeding or starting iron or B12, new cells differ in size from old ones.
A high RDW is a clue, not a diagnosis. It helps tell early iron shortage from thalassaemia trait.
RDW is non-specific and is mainly useful alongside MCV and iron or B12 tests.
Talk to a doctor if RDW is high together with low haemoglobin or abnormal MCV.
This result shows what share of your white blood cells are neutrophils. They are the most common type and the first responders to bacterial infections.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Neutrophils are the most common white cell. They are the first to arrive at a bacterial infection or injury and swallow germs.
This result is the share of all your white cells that are this type, so it moves when other types change. The absolute count is usually more useful.
Neutrophils help show whether the body is fighting a bacterial infection or physical stress, and a low count shows how well protected you are against infection.

A lower neutrophil percentage can come from viral infections, some medicines, low B12 or folate, or bone marrow problems. It can also be naturally lower in some healthy people, including many people of African, Middle Eastern or South Asian descent.
Your neutrophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher neutrophil percentage is most often caused by a bacterial infection, inflammation, injury, physical stress, smoking or steroid medicines.
Your report did not include a reference range for neutrophil percentage, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Bacterial infection: The marrow releases extra neutrophils to fight bacteria, so the count rises.
Physical stress, injury or surgery: Stress hormones push neutrophils from the vessel walls into the bloodstream.
Smoking: Smoking keeps the body in a low-grade inflamed state, raising neutrophils.
Steroid medicines: Steroids raise the neutrophil count.
Viral infections: Some viral infections, including dengue, temporarily lower neutrophils.
Some medicines: Some antibiotics, thyroid medicines and cancer treatments can lower neutrophils.
Low B12 or folate: The marrow needs these vitamins to make all blood cells.
Inherited lower counts: Many healthy people of South Asian, African or Middle Eastern descent naturally have lower neutrophils without extra infections.
A slightly low neutrophil count in a well person is often a normal variation, especially in people of South Asian descent, but it is still worth a doctor's view if it persists.
Percentages depend on the other white cell types, so the absolute count is usually more useful.
Talk to a doctor if your neutrophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
This result shows what share of your white blood cells are eosinophils. They help fight parasites and take part in allergic reactions such as asthma and hay fever.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Eosinophils fight parasites, such as worms, and take part in allergic reactions such as asthma, hay fever and eczema.
This result is the share of all your white cells that are this type, so it moves when other types change. The absolute count is usually more useful.
Eosinophils help point to allergy or a parasite infection when they are raised.
A lower eosinophil percentage is usually not a concern. It can fall with stress, steroid medicines or the body's response to infection.
Your eosinophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher eosinophil percentage is most often caused by allergies, asthma, eczema or parasite infections. Some medicines can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for eosinophil percentage, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Allergy, asthma or eczema: Allergic reactions call eosinophils into the blood and tissues.
Parasite infections: Worm infections, common in India, strongly raise eosinophils.
Some medicines: Some medicines cause an allergic-type reaction that raises eosinophils.
Steroid medicines and acute stress: Steroids and stress hormones lower eosinophils.
High eosinophils are not always allergy. Worm infections are a common cause in India, so a doctor may check stool or treat for worms.
Percentages depend on the other white cell types, so the absolute count is usually more useful.
Talk to a doctor if your eosinophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
This result shows what share of your white blood cells are lymphocytes. They include cells that make antibodies and cells that fight viruses.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Lymphocytes include the cells that make antibodies and the cells that kill virus-infected cells. They also remember past infections.
This result is the share of all your white cells that are this type, so it moves when other types change. The absolute count is usually more useful.
Lymphocytes help show a recent viral infection and, when low, how well the immune system can respond.
A lower lymphocyte percentage can happen during acute illness, stress, with steroid medicines, or with conditions that weaken immunity.
Your lymphocytes result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher lymphocyte percentage is often seen during or after a viral infection. Less often, it can be due to a long-lasting infection or a blood condition.
Your report did not include a reference range for lymphocyte percentage, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Viral infections: Lymphocytes multiply to fight viruses, so the count rises during and after a viral illness.
Long-lasting infections: Infections such as tuberculosis can raise lymphocytes.
Acute illness and stress: Severe illness and stress hormones lower lymphocytes for a while.
Steroid medicines: Steroids lower the lymphocyte count.
Conditions that weaken immunity: Some infections, such as HIV, and some treatments reduce lymphocytes.
Blood conditions: Less often, a raised count comes from a blood condition, especially in older adults.
A raised lymphocyte count after a cold or fever is usually the immune system doing its job.
Percentages depend on the other white cell types, so the absolute count is usually more useful.
Talk to a doctor if your lymphocytes result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
This result shows what share of your white blood cells are monocytes. They clean up germs and damaged cells and help with healing.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Monocytes travel to tissues, where they become clean-up cells that swallow germs and dead cells and help healing.
This result is the share of all your white cells that are this type, so it moves when other types change. The absolute count is usually more useful.
Monocytes help show recovery from infection or a long-lasting infection or inflammation.
A lower monocyte percentage is usually not a concern on its own. It can be seen with steroid medicines or some bone marrow problems.
Your monocytes result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher monocyte percentage can be seen while recovering from infection, with ongoing infections or inflammation, or, less often, with some blood conditions.
Your report did not include a reference range for monocyte percentage, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Recovery from infection: Monocytes often rise as the body clears an infection.
Long-lasting infections: Infections such as tuberculosis raise monocytes.
Inflammatory conditions: Ongoing inflammation, such as inflammatory bowel disease, raises them.
Steroid medicines: Steroids lower monocytes.
Bone marrow conditions: Less often, a persistent change comes from the bone marrow.
A mildly high monocyte count after an infection is common and often settles on its own.
Percentages depend on the other white cell types, so the absolute count is usually more useful.
Talk to a doctor if your monocytes result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
This result shows what share of your white blood cells are basophils. They are the least common type and are involved in allergic reactions and inflammation.
White blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones.
Basophils are the rarest white cell. They release histamine and other chemicals during allergic reactions and inflammation.
This result is the share of all your white cells that are this type, so it moves when other types change. The absolute count is usually more useful.
Basophils are rarely important alone; a persistently raised count can sometimes point to allergy or a bone marrow condition.
A lower basophil percentage is common and usually not a concern, as basophils are normally very few.
Your basophils result is inside the lab's range, suggesting this part of your immune system looks balanced.
A higher basophil percentage can be seen with allergies, ongoing inflammation, an underactive thyroid or, rarely, some bone marrow conditions.
Your report did not include a reference range for basophil percentage, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Allergy: Allergic reactions can raise basophils slightly.
Ongoing inflammation: Long-term inflammation can raise them.
Underactive thyroid: An underactive thyroid is sometimes linked with higher basophils.
Bone marrow conditions: A persistently high count can rarely come from the bone marrow.
A low basophil count is not a problem. They are normally so few that zero is a common result.
Percentages depend on the other white cell types, so the absolute count is usually more useful.
Talk to a doctor if your basophils result is clearly abnormal, keeps being abnormal, or comes with fever, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising or frequent infections.
RDW-CV shows how much your red blood cells vary in size, expressed as a percentage of their average size.
Healthy red cells are mostly a similar size.
When new cells are made under strain, for example with low iron or B12, sizes become more mixed.
A high RDW can be an early clue to low iron or low B12, sometimes before haemoglobin falls.
A low RDW is not a concern.
Your RDW is inside the lab's range, suggesting your red cells are a fairly even size.
A higher RDW means red cells are more mixed in size. It is commonly seen with low iron, low B12 or folate, or recovery from blood loss.
Your report did not include a reference range for relative red cell size variation (RDW-CV), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: As iron runs low, new cells are smaller than old ones, so sizes vary more.
Vitamin B12 and folate: Shortages produce larger cells alongside normal ones.
Recent blood loss or treatment: After bleeding or starting iron or B12, new cells differ in size from old ones.
A high RDW is a clue, not a diagnosis. It helps tell early iron shortage from thalassaemia trait.
RDW is non-specific and is mainly useful alongside MCV and iron or B12 tests.
Talk to a doctor if RDW is high together with low haemoglobin or abnormal MCV.
The Mentzer index is a calculation that divides your red cell size (MCV) by your red cell count. Doctors use it as a rough first clue when red cells are small.
Both low iron and thalassaemia trait make red cells small.
Thalassaemia trait tends to give many small cells, while low iron tends to give fewer.
When red cells are small, the index helps decide which tests to do next.
This index is worked out from your red cell results. The lab's formula and cut-off are not confirmed, so CURA does not label it high or low. It only matters if your red cells are small.
A higher index leans towards low iron as the cause of small red cells.
A lower index leans towards thalassaemia trait, an inherited condition, as the cause of small red cells.
Your index falls in the lab's range. It is only meaningful when your red cells are small.
Red cell measurements: This index is calculated from the red cell results above, so it changes when they change.
Iron level: Iron shortage and thalassaemia trait push the result in different directions, which is why the index exists.
Calculation method: The index is MCV divided by the red cell count; the method and cut-offs your lab used are not confirmed.
These indices only suggest whether iron shortage or thalassaemia trait is more likely. Neither can be confirmed without other tests.
The index is a screening clue, not a diagnosis. It can be wrong, especially if low iron and thalassaemia trait occur together.
Talk to a doctor if your red cells are small. Iron tests or haemoglobin studies may be needed to confirm the cause.
The red blood cell count shows how many red blood cells are in a small amount of your blood. Red cells carry oxygen around your body.
Red cells are made in the bone marrow and live about four months.
Your body needs iron, B12 and folate to make them.
The count helps check for anaemia, dehydration and conditions where too many red cells are made.
A lower red cell count usually goes with anaemia, caused for example by low iron, low B12 or folate, or blood loss.
Your red cell count is inside the lab's range.
A higher red cell count can come from dehydration, smoking, high altitude, lung conditions or thalassaemia trait, where there are many small cells.
Your report did not include a reference range for red blood cell count, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Hydration: Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises the count.
Iron, B12 and folate: Shortages reduce red cell production.
Smoking: Smoking raises red cell production.
Altitude: Living high up raises red cells.
Thalassaemia trait: This trait often gives a high count of small cells with a normal or slightly low haemoglobin.
A high red cell count with small cells is a classic clue to thalassaemia trait, not to having too much blood.
The count is read together with haemoglobin and red cell size; on its own it cannot show the cause.
Diets low in iron or B12 can lower red cell production over time.
Talk to a doctor if the count is abnormal along with abnormal haemoglobin or tiredness.
The GK index is a calculation from your red cell results. Like the Mentzer index, doctors sometimes use it to tell low iron apart from thalassaemia trait when red cells are small.
The GK index combines red cell size, haemoglobin and red cell count into one number.
The GK index is only meaningful when red cells are small.
The GK index can help decide whether iron tests or thalassaemia tests should come next.
This index is worked out from your red cell results. The lab's formula and cut-off are not confirmed, so CURA does not label it high or low. It only matters if your red cells are small.
A higher index leans towards low iron as the cause of small red cells.
A lower index leans towards thalassaemia trait.
Your index falls in the lab's range. It matters only if your red cells are small.
Red cell measurements: This index is calculated from the red cell results above, so it changes when they change.
Iron level: Iron shortage and thalassaemia trait push the result in different directions, which is why the index exists.
Calculation method: The index is a formula using MCV, haemoglobin and the red cell count; the method and cut-offs your lab used are not confirmed.
These indices only suggest whether iron shortage or thalassaemia trait is more likely. Neither can be confirmed without other tests.
The GK index is a screening clue only and can be wrong; confirmation needs iron or haemoglobin studies.
Talk to a doctor if your red cells are small, so the cause can be confirmed with the right tests.
RDWI is a calculation that combines red cell size, size variation and red cell count. It is another screening clue used when red cells are small.
RDWI uses MCV, RDW and the red cell count.
Like the Mentzer and GK indices, it helps compare low iron with thalassaemia trait.
RDWI can help decide which tests to do next when red cells are small.
This index is worked out from your red cell results. The lab's formula and cut-off are not confirmed, so CURA does not label it high or low. It only matters if your red cells are small.
A higher RDWI leans towards low iron as the cause of small red cells.
A lower RDWI leans towards thalassaemia trait.
Your RDWI falls in the lab's range. It matters only if your red cells are small.
Red cell measurements: This index is calculated from the red cell results above, so it changes when they change.
Iron level: Iron shortage and thalassaemia trait push the result in different directions, which is why the index exists.
Calculation method: The index is MCV and RDW multiplied and divided by the red cell count; the method and cut-offs your lab used are not confirmed.
These indices only suggest whether iron shortage or thalassaemia trait is more likely. Neither can be confirmed without other tests.
RDWI is a screening clue only; confirmation needs iron or haemoglobin studies.
Talk to a doctor if your red cells are small, so the cause can be confirmed.
Fasting blood sugar measures the amount of glucose, a type of sugar, in your blood after at least 8 hours without food.
Food is broken down into glucose, which your cells use for energy.
Insulin, a hormone from the pancreas, moves glucose from the blood into your cells.
Overnight, your liver releases stored glucose to keep levels steady, so a fasting sample shows your baseline.
Fasting blood sugar is one of the main tests used to check for prediabetes and diabetes.
A lower fasting sugar can follow a long fast, heavy exercise, alcohol or diabetes medicines. It can cause shakiness, sweating and confusion.

Your fasting sugar is inside the healthy range, suggesting your body kept blood sugar steady overnight. A result below the diabetes threshold on one test does not rule out diabetes on its own. Doctors confirm or exclude it with repeat or additional tests, especially if you have symptoms or risk factors.

A higher fasting sugar can mean your body is not responding well to insulin or is not making enough. It can also rise if you ate before the test, were unwell or stressed, or take some medicines such as steroids.
Your report did not include a reference range for fasting blood sugar, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Food before the test: Eating or drinking anything other than water within 8 hours raises the result, so it no longer shows a true fasting level.
Insulin resistance: When cells respond poorly to insulin, the liver releases more glucose overnight and fasting sugar creeps up.
Body weight: Extra weight, especially around the waist, makes insulin work less well.
Illness or stress: Stress hormones during illness or strain push blood sugar up.
Steroids and some other medicines: Steroids, some water tablets and some antipsychotic medicines raise blood sugar.
Sleep: Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.

The lab range for fasting sugar is not the same as the diagnostic thresholds. Doctors use 100 to 125 mg/dL for prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or above for diabetes, and usually confirm diabetes with a second test.
Feeling well does not mean blood sugar is normal. Prediabetes and early diabetes usually cause no symptoms.
One fasting sugar result is a snapshot. Diabetes is usually confirmed with a repeat test or HbA1c.
Keep up what helps: regular activity, meals built around vegetables, dal and whole grains, and few sugary drinks.
A good result now does not mean blood sugar stays the same. Risk rises with age, weight gain and family history, so check again at the interval your doctor suggests.
Indians tend to develop type 2 diabetes at a younger age and lower weight than many other groups, so waist size and activity matter even if you are not overweight.
Lifestyle changes can delay or prevent type 2 diabetes in people with prediabetes.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and pair rice or roti with dal, curd, paneer, eggs or other protein. This slows how quickly sugar enters your blood.
Swap sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour for water, whole fruit and whole grains like millets or brown rice. These cause smaller sugar spikes.
Take a 10 to 15 minute walk after main meals. Physical activity helps your body manage blood sugar, and sugar after a walk is often lower than before.
Aim for enough sleep. A healthy weight, regular activity and enough sleep are part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Diet, activity, sleep and body weight all affect how well insulin works and so your fasting sugar.
Talk to a doctor if your blood sugar results are above range, so they can check for prediabetes or diabetes. Both are common and often have no symptoms.
Seek care promptly if you have extreme thirst, passing a lot of urine, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, or feel shaky, sweaty or confused from low sugar.
HbA1c shows your average blood sugar over roughly the past two to three months. It measures how much sugar has stuck to the haemoglobin in your red blood cells.
Glucose in your blood naturally sticks to haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells.
The more sugar in your blood over time, the more sticks.
Red cells live about three months, so HbA1c gives a longer view than a single sugar test.
HbA1c is used to diagnose prediabetes and diabetes and to see how well diabetes is controlled.
A lower HbA1c is usually not a concern. If you take diabetes medicines, ask your doctor what a low result means for you. Recent blood loss or a transfusion can also make it read low.

Your HbA1c is inside the healthy range, so your average blood sugar over the past few months has been healthy. Keep up the habits that support it, because risk can change over time. A result below the diabetes threshold on one test does not rule out diabetes on its own. Doctors confirm or exclude it with repeat or additional tests, especially if you have symptoms or risk factors.

A higher HbA1c means your blood sugar has been running higher over recent months, which can mean prediabetes or diabetes. It is linked with a higher risk of heart, kidney, eye and nerve problems over time.
Your report did not include a reference range for HbA1c (long-term blood sugar), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Average blood sugar: The higher your blood sugar over the past two to three months, the more sugar sticks to haemoglobin.
Diet and activity: Meals low in sugary and refined foods and regular activity lower average sugar over months.
Body weight: Extra weight makes insulin work less well, raising average sugar.
Very low iron: Very low iron can make HbA1c read falsely high.
Recent blood loss or transfusion: These replace old red cells with new ones, which can make HbA1c read too low.
Kidney failure: Kidney failure can make HbA1c read too high or too low.
Inherited haemoglobin variants: Some inherited types of haemoglobin, more common in some families, interfere with certain lab methods.

Labs often print 4.0 to 5.6% as the normal range. Doctors use separate diagnostic thresholds: 5.7 to 6.4% suggests prediabetes and 6.5% or above suggests diabetes, usually confirmed with a repeat test.
A normal HbA1c does not mean nothing else needs attention. It says nothing about cholesterol, blood pressure, weight or liver fat.
HbA1c is an average. It cannot show sugar spikes after meals or drops in between.
Very low iron can make HbA1c read falsely high. Recent blood loss, kidney failure and some inherited types of haemoglobin can make it read too high or too low.
Keep up what helps: regular activity, meals built around vegetables, dal and whole grains, and few sugary drinks.
A good result now does not mean blood sugar stays the same. Risk rises with age, weight gain and family history, so check again at the interval your doctor suggests.
Indians tend to develop type 2 diabetes at a younger age and lower weight than many other groups, so waist size and activity matter even if you are not overweight.
Lifestyle changes can delay or prevent type 2 diabetes in people with prediabetes.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and pair rice or roti with dal, curd, paneer, eggs or other protein. This slows how quickly sugar enters your blood.
Swap sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour for water, whole fruit and whole grains like millets or brown rice. These cause smaller sugar spikes.
Take a 10 to 15 minute walk after main meals. Physical activity helps your body manage blood sugar, and sugar after a walk is often lower than before.
Aim for enough sleep. A healthy weight, regular activity and enough sleep are part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Regular activity, fewer sugary and refined foods, good sleep and a healthy weight can all bring HbA1c down over time.
Talk to a doctor if your blood sugar results are above range, so they can check for prediabetes or diabetes. Both are common and often have no symptoms.
Seek care promptly if you have extreme thirst, passing a lot of urine, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, or feel shaky, sweaty or confused from low sugar.
Fasting insulin measures how much insulin is in your blood after not eating. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from your blood into your cells.
Your pancreas releases insulin even between meals to keep sugar steady.
If your cells respond poorly to insulin, the pancreas makes more to keep sugar normal. This is called insulin resistance.
So insulin can rise years before blood sugar does.
A high fasting insulin can be an early sign of insulin resistance, which raises the chance of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver and PCOS.
A lower fasting insulin with normal sugar is usually fine. Low insulin with high sugar can mean the pancreas is not making enough.
Your fasting insulin is inside the lab's range.

A higher fasting insulin often means your body needs more insulin to keep sugar normal, a sign of insulin resistance. Extra weight around the waist, low activity and poor sleep are common contributors.
Your report did not include a reference range for fasting insulin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Insulin resistance: When cells respond poorly, the pancreas makes more insulin to keep sugar normal, so fasting insulin rises before sugar does.
Waist size and body weight: Fat around the waist is closely linked with insulin resistance.
Physical activity: Not being active is a risk factor for insulin resistance; regular activity helps.
Sleep: Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Food before the test: Eating raises insulin, so a non-fasting sample reads high.
Some medicines: Steroids and some others raise insulin; insulin injections make the result unreliable.
There is no agreed cut-off for fasting insulin. It is a clue to insulin resistance, not a diagnosis.
Insulin tests are not standardised between labs, and one result cannot diagnose insulin resistance.
Keep up what helps: regular activity, meals built around vegetables, dal and whole grains, and few sugary drinks.
A good result now does not mean blood sugar stays the same. Risk rises with age, weight gain and family history, so check again at the interval your doctor suggests.
Indians tend to develop type 2 diabetes at a younger age and lower weight than many other groups, so waist size and activity matter even if you are not overweight.
Lifestyle changes can delay or prevent type 2 diabetes in people with prediabetes.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and pair rice or roti with dal, curd, paneer, eggs or other protein. This slows how quickly sugar enters your blood.
Swap sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour for water, whole fruit and whole grains like millets or brown rice. These cause smaller sugar spikes.
Take a 10 to 15 minute walk after main meals. Physical activity helps your body manage blood sugar, and sugar after a walk is often lower than before.
Aim for enough sleep. A healthy weight, regular activity and enough sleep are part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Regular activity, especially strength exercise, losing extra weight around the waist and better sleep help your cells respond to insulin.
Talk to a doctor if fasting insulin is high, especially with high sugar, a large waist, irregular periods or signs of fatty liver.
Average blood sugar is a blood sugar value that represents an average over time, rather than one moment. Many labs calculate it from your HbA1c.
Blood sugar rises and falls through the day.
When worked out from HbA1c, this value turns your HbA1c into everyday glucose units, covering roughly the past two to three months.
Average blood sugar makes HbA1c easier to compare with day-to-day sugar readings.
The way this lab calculates average blood sugar is not confirmed, so CURA does not label it high or low. Look at your HbA1c, which this value is usually based on.
HbA1c: This value is usually calculated from HbA1c, so it follows it exactly.
Calculation method: Labs use different formulas, and your lab's method is not confirmed.
This number is not a measured sugar reading. It is HbA1c converted into sugar units.
The lab's calculation method is not confirmed, so this value is shown for information only. Your HbA1c is the result to rely on.
Use your HbA1c result and discuss it with a doctor if it is above range.
Urine pH shows how acidic or alkaline your urine is. Your kidneys adjust it to keep your blood's acid balance steady.
A lower number means more acidic urine, and a higher number means more alkaline urine.
Diet changes urine pH: meat tends to make it more acidic, while vegetables and fruit make it more alkaline.
Urine pH can help explain kidney stones and infections and is part of routine urine testing.
More acidic urine can follow a high-protein diet, dehydration, fasting or uncontrolled diabetes. It can favour uric acid stones.
Your urine pH is inside the lab's range.
More alkaline urine can follow a vegetable-rich diet, some urine infections or some medicines. It can favour certain types of kidney stones.
Your report did not include a reference range for urine acidity (pH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Diet: Meat-heavy diets make urine more acidic; fruit- and vegetable-rich diets make it less acidic.
Hydration: Concentrated urine is often more acidic.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Kidney function: Kidneys balance acid by changing urine pH, so some kidney conditions alter it.
Some medicines: Antacids and some other medicines change urine pH.
Urine pH does not show the acidity of your blood or body. Blood pH stays tightly controlled whatever the urine shows.
Urine results can change with how the sample was collected, how concentrated it was and how long it waited before testing.
Enough water and plenty of vegetables and fruit help keep urine pH in a comfortable range.
Drink water regularly through the day. Well-diluted urine lowers the chance of stones whatever the pH.
Diets high in meat make urine more acidic; fruit and vegetables make it more alkaline.
Talk to a doctor if you have had kidney stones or urine infections and your pH is outside the range.
Urobilinogen is a substance made in the gut from bilirubin, the yellow pigment from old red blood cells. A small amount normally appears in urine.
Bilirubin from the liver passes into the gut, where bacteria turn it into urobilinogen.
Some is reabsorbed into the blood and passes out in urine.
Changes can point to liver problems, red cell breakdown or blocked bile flow.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Liver function: When the liver struggles to clear urobilinogen from the blood, more appears in urine.
Red blood cell breakdown: Faster red cell breakdown makes more bilirubin, and more urobilinogen.
Bile flow: If bile cannot reach the gut, gut bacteria make no urobilinogen, so it disappears from urine.
Antibiotics: Antibiotics reduce the gut bacteria that make urobilinogen.
Small amounts of urobilinogen in urine are normal.
Urobilinogen is a screening clue only; blood liver tests give a clearer picture.
Talk to a doctor if urobilinogen is abnormal together with yellow eyes or skin, dark urine or pale stools.
Urine colour describes how your urine sample looked. Pale yellow is typical.
Urine gets its colour from a pigment called urochrome.
Drinking less makes urine darker, and drinking more makes it paler.
Colour gives quick clues about hydration and, sometimes, blood, bile or medicines in the urine.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Hydration: Less water makes urine darker yellow; more water makes it paler.
Foods such as beetroot: Beetroot, berries and some food colours can tint urine pink or red.
Vitamins and medicines: B vitamins make urine bright yellow; some medicines turn it orange, green or blue.
Blood or bile in urine: Blood makes urine pink, red or cola-coloured; bile pigments make it dark brown.
Dark urine is not always dehydration. Dark brown urine with yellow eyes can mean a liver or bile problem.
Colour alone cannot identify the cause of a change.
Pale yellow urine is a simple sign you are drinking enough.
Drink water regularly. Pale yellow urine is a simple sign of good hydration.
Hydration, some foods and B vitamins change urine colour.
See a doctor if urine is red, brown or cola-coloured without an obvious food or medicine cause, or dark with yellow eyes.
Urine clarity describes whether your urine sample was clear or cloudy.
Fresh urine is usually clear.
Cloudiness can come from crystals, cells, bacteria, mucus or simply from the sample cooling.
Cloudy urine can be a clue to infection or crystals, but often has a harmless cause.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Sample standing time: Urine left standing becomes cloudy as crystals form and bacteria grow.
Crystals: Phosphate and urate crystals, often harmless, cloud urine.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Mucus or cells: Mucus and lining cells make urine hazy.
Diet: Some foods raise phosphate in urine and cloud it.
Cloudy urine is not always infection. Crystals and standing time are common reasons.
Clarity alone cannot show the cause; microscopy results help.
See a doctor if you have burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, fever or pain in your back or side.
This checks whether sugar (glucose) is present in your urine. Normally there is little or none.
Your kidneys filter sugar but usually reabsorb all of it.
When blood sugar is very high, the kidneys cannot keep up and sugar spills into urine.
Sugar in the urine can be a sign of high blood sugar or diabetes.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Sugar in urine can mean blood sugar has been high, or that the kidneys pass sugar more easily. Some diabetes medicines do this on purpose.
No sugar was found. This does not rule out diabetes, which is checked with blood tests.
Blood sugar level: Kidneys let sugar into urine once blood sugar rises above about 180 mg/dL.
Diabetes medicines called SGLT2 inhibitors: These medicines deliberately pass sugar into urine.
Pregnancy: Kidneys let more sugar through in pregnancy.
Kidney handling of sugar: A few people have kidneys that let sugar through at normal blood sugar levels.
No sugar in urine does not mean blood sugar is normal. It only appears once blood sugar is quite high.
Urine sugar does not measure current blood sugar and is not used to diagnose diabetes.
Talk to a doctor if sugar is found in your urine, so your blood sugar can be checked. Note that some diabetes medicines cause sugar in urine on purpose.
This dipstick test looks for traces of blood in your urine, which may not be visible to the eye.
The test reacts with haemoglobin from red blood cells.
The test can also react with myoglobin, a muscle protein released after muscle injury.
Blood in urine can come from infection, stones, hard exercise, periods or, less often, kidney or bladder disease.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Traces of blood were detected. Periods, infection, stones and hard exercise are common causes, and a repeat test is usually advised.
No blood was detected by the dipstick.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Kidney stones: Stones scratch the lining of the urinary tract and cause bleeding.
Menstrual blood: A sample during or near a period often contains blood.
Hard exercise: Strenuous exercise can cause a little blood in urine for a day or two.
Muscle injury: Damaged muscle releases myoglobin, which the strip reads as blood.
A positive strip without red cells under the microscope may be myoglobin, a protein released from damaged muscle, not blood.
The dipstick does not show where the blood comes from, and a positive test needs microscopy and often a repeat sample.
Talk to a doctor if blood is found in your urine and you were not on your period, especially if you are over 40, smoke or see visible blood.
This counts red blood cells seen under a microscope in your urine sample. A few can be normal.
Red cells can enter urine anywhere from the kidneys to the bladder.
Microscopy confirms what a dipstick blood test suggests.
More than a few red cells can point to infection, stones, injury or kidney or bladder conditions.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Kidney stones: Stones cause bleeding from the urinary lining.
Menstrual blood: Period blood can enter the sample.
