Hard exercise: Strenuous exercise can add red cells to urine briefly.
Kidney or bladder conditions: Kidney inflammation and, less often, growths in the bladder or kidney cause bleeding.
Blood in urine that you cannot see still needs a repeat test, especially in people over 40 or smokers.
Microscopy does not show the source of the bleeding.
Talk to a doctor if red cells are reported in your urine and you were not on your period, especially if you are over 40 or smoke.
This counts white blood cells, sometimes called pus cells, seen in your urine sample. A few can be normal.
White cells fight infection.
Many white cells in urine usually mean there is inflammation or infection in the urinary tract.
Raised white cells in urine are a common sign of a urine infection.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Sample contamination: If the first part of the stream or skin touches the sample, cells and bacteria from outside the bladder get in. A clean midstream sample avoids this.
Kidney inflammation: Inflamed kidneys release white cells into urine.
Sexually transmitted infections: Infections of the urethra release white cells.
Pus cells without symptoms are often contamination, and do not always need antibiotics.
White cells can come from skin or vaginal contamination if the sample was not a clean midstream catch.
See a doctor if you have burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, fever or pain in your back or side.
Epithelial cells are cells from the lining of the urinary tract or skin, seen in your urine sample.
Small numbers are normal as linings shed old cells.
Many cells usually mean the sample picked up skin cells during collection.
Epithelial cells mainly help the lab judge sample quality.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Sample collection technique: Lining cells from the skin around the urethra enter a sample that is not midstream.
Inflammation of the urinary tract: Inflamed linings shed more cells.
A few lining cells are normal and usually reflect how the sample was collected.
A high count usually reflects contamination rather than disease.
Usually no action is needed. Repeat with a clean midstream sample if many cells are reported.
Crystals are tiny solid particles that can form in urine from minerals and salts.
Crystals form when urine is concentrated or its acid balance favours them.
Many types are harmless and appear when the sample cools.
Some crystal types can be linked with kidney stones.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Hydration: Concentrated urine lets crystals form.
Diet: Foods rich in oxalate, such as spinach and nuts, or purines can add crystals.
Urine pH: Different crystals form in acidic and alkaline urine.
Sample cooling: Crystals form as urine cools in the container, so many are not present in the body.
Crystals in a sample are not kidney stones. Many form only after the urine has cooled.
Crystals in a sample do not mean you have or will get kidney stones.
Drinking enough water keeps urine dilute, which makes crystals less likely to form.
Drink water regularly through the day. Dilute urine makes crystals less likely to form.
Concentrated urine from low fluid intake makes crystals more likely.
Talk to a doctor if you have had kidney stones, or have side or back pain, and crystals are reported.
Casts are tiny tube-shaped particles formed in the kidney's small tubes and washed out in urine.
Casts take the shape of the tubes they form in.
Clear (hyaline) casts can appear after exercise or dehydration. Other types can point to kidney problems.
Some cast types are a clue to kidney inflammation or damage.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Exercise: Hard exercise can produce a few harmless casts.
Dehydration: Concentrated urine favours cast formation.
Kidney conditions: Some casts, especially those containing cells, form inside damaged kidney tubules.
A few clear casts are often harmless; casts containing cells need a doctor's view.
The type of cast matters, and the report may not always specify it.
Talk to a doctor if casts other than a few clear casts are reported, especially with protein or blood in the urine.
This reports whether bacteria were seen in your urine sample.
Urine in the bladder is normally free of bacteria.
Bacteria can come from a urine infection or from skin during collection.
Bacteria with symptoms or white cells can point to a urine infection.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Urine infection: Bacteria in the bladder or kidneys cause inflammation, which this finding can pick up.
Sample contamination: If the first part of the stream or skin touches the sample, cells and bacteria from outside the bladder get in. A clean midstream sample avoids this.
Delay before testing: Bacteria multiply in urine left at room temperature, so delays raise the count.
Bacteria in urine without symptoms usually do not need antibiotics, except in pregnancy or before some procedures.
Bacteria without symptoms often do not need treatment, except in pregnancy and some other situations. A urine culture confirms infection.
See a doctor if you have burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, fever or pain in your back or side.
This reports whether yeast, a type of fungus, was seen in your urine sample.
Yeast can live harmlessly on skin and in the vagina.
Yeast can enter a sample during collection or, less often, cause infection.
Yeast can be more common with diabetes, after antibiotics or in pregnancy.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Sample contamination: If the first part of the stream or skin touches the sample, cells and bacteria from outside the bladder get in. A clean midstream sample avoids this.
Diabetes or high blood sugar: Sugar in urine feeds yeast.
Recent antibiotics: Antibiotics clear normal bacteria and let yeast grow.
Pregnancy: Hormone changes make yeast infections more common.
Yeast in a sample is often from the skin or vagina rather than the bladder.
Yeast in a sample is often contamination and does not always mean infection.
Talk to a doctor if yeast is reported with urinary symptoms, or if you have diabetes.
This item is labelled nitrate on your report. The standard urine dipstick test checks for nitrite, which some bacteria make. The lab needs to confirm which test was done.
Some bacteria that cause urine infections turn nitrate from food into nitrite.
A positive nitrite test can support a urine infection.
Nitrite testing is one of the quick screening checks for urine infection.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Urine infection: Many bacteria that cause urine infections turn nitrate into nitrite, which the strip detects.
Time the urine stayed in the bladder: Bacteria need about four hours to make nitrite, so first-morning urine is best.
Diet: Low vegetable intake means less nitrate in urine to convert.
A negative nitrite does not rule out infection. Some bacteria do not make it.
The test identity is not confirmed, and a negative nitrite does not rule out infection.
See a doctor if you have burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, fever or pain in your back or side.
This checks for ketones in your urine. Ketones are made when your body burns fat for energy instead of sugar.
When you fast, eat very few carbohydrates or are unwell, your body burns more fat and makes ketones.
In diabetes, a lack of insulin can make ketones build up dangerously.
Ketones can show fasting or low-carbohydrate eating, but in diabetes they can be a warning sign.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Ketones were found. Fasting, low-carbohydrate eating, vomiting or illness are common causes. In diabetes, ketones need prompt medical attention.
No ketones were found.
Fasting: When you do not eat, the body burns fat and makes ketones.
Low-carbohydrate diets: Very low carbohydrate eating makes the body switch to fat for fuel.
Vomiting or illness: Not keeping food down raises ketones.
Diabetes: Without enough insulin, cells cannot use sugar and burn fat, producing ketones; high levels in diabetes can be dangerous.
Intense exercise: Long hard exercise raises ketones.
Ketones after fasting are expected, but ketones with high blood sugar in diabetes need urgent care.
Urine ketones show recent fat burning, not how serious it is.
Seek urgent care if you have diabetes and ketones with vomiting, tummy pain, fast breathing or confusion.
This checks for protein in your urine. Healthy kidneys keep almost all protein in the blood.
Kidney filters hold back protein while letting waste pass.
When filters are damaged, protein leaks into urine.
Protein in urine can be an early sign of kidney damage, especially with diabetes or high blood pressure.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Protein was found. It can be temporary after fever or exercise, but if it persists it can mean kidney damage.
No protein was found by the dipstick. Small amounts may need a more sensitive test.
Kidney filter damage: Healthy filters keep protein in the blood; damaged ones let it leak.
Diabetes: High blood sugar over years damages the filters.
High blood pressure: Long-term high pressure damages the filters.
Fever or hard exercise: Both can cause a brief, harmless rise.
Urine infection: Infection can add protein to urine.
One positive protein strip after exercise or fever is often temporary, so it is repeated before drawing conclusions.
A dipstick can miss small amounts. A urine albumin to creatinine ratio test is more sensitive.
Talk to a doctor if protein is found in your urine, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure, swelling or foamy urine.
Leukocyte esterase is a substance released by white blood cells. A positive test suggests white cells, and possibly infection, in the urine.
White cells fight infection and release this enzyme.
The dipstick changes colour when it detects the enzyme.
Leukocyte esterase is a quick screening check for urine infection.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
White cell activity was detected, which can point to a urine infection or inflammation.
No white cell activity was detected.
Urine infection: White cells release this enzyme, so a positive strip suggests white cells are present.
Sample contamination: If the first part of the stream or skin touches the sample, cells and bacteria from outside the bladder get in. A clean midstream sample avoids this.
Kidney inflammation: Inflamed kidneys release white cells.
A positive strip alone does not confirm infection; symptoms and culture matter.
A positive result can come from contamination, and a negative result does not rule out infection.
See a doctor if you have burning when passing urine, needing to go often, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, fever or pain in your back or side.
This checks for bile pigments, mainly bilirubin, in your urine. Normally none is found.
Bilirubin is a yellow pigment processed by the liver.
When the liver or bile ducts are not working well, processed bilirubin can spill into urine and make it dark.
Bile pigments in urine can be an early sign of liver or bile duct problems.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Bile pigments were found, which can point to a liver or bile duct problem.
No bile pigments were found.
Liver inflammation: An inflamed liver lets processed bilirubin into the blood, and kidneys pass it into urine.
Bile duct blockage: When bile cannot drain, processed bilirubin spills into urine and darkens it.
Sample exposed to light: Bilirubin breaks down in light, so a delayed sample can read falsely negative.
Bile in urine is never normal. Dark urine with yellow eyes needs prompt medical advice.
The result can be falsely negative if the sample was left in light.
See a doctor if bile pigments are found, especially with dark urine, yellow eyes or skin, or pale stools.
Urine specific gravity shows how concentrated your urine is. It is a quick guide to how well hydrated you are and how well your kidneys concentrate urine.
When you drink less, your kidneys hold on to water and urine becomes more concentrated.
When you drink more, urine becomes more dilute.
Urine concentration helps judge hydration and can hint at kidney or hormone problems.
A lower specific gravity means dilute urine, usually from drinking a lot. If it stays low, it can mean the kidneys are not concentrating urine well.
Your urine concentration is inside the lab's range.
A higher specific gravity usually means concentrated urine from not drinking enough, sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea. Sugar or protein in the urine can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for urine concentration (specific gravity), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Fluid intake: Drinking less water makes urine more concentrated; drinking a lot dilutes it.
Sweating: Heat and exercise lose water through sweat, concentrating urine.
Vomiting or diarrhoea: Fluid loss concentrates urine.
Sugar or protein in urine: Dissolved sugar or protein raises the reading.
Kidney function: Kidneys that cannot concentrate urine give a fixed, dilute reading.
Very pale urine all the time is not always healthier. Drinking far more than you need can dilute body salts.
Urine results can change with how the sample was collected, how concentrated it was and how long it waited before testing.
Drinking water steadily through the day, more in hot weather, keeps urine pale yellow.
Drink water regularly, more in hot weather or when active. Pale yellow urine is a simple sign you are drinking enough.
How much you drink is the main everyday influence.
Talk to a doctor if your urine is always very dilute even when you drink little, or always very concentrated despite drinking well.
This records the volume of the urine sample that was tested. It describes the sample, not how much urine you pass in a day.
Labs note the sample volume to check there was enough to test.
Urine sample volume helps the lab judge whether the sample was adequate.
A small sample can limit how much testing the lab can do.
The sample volume was adequate for testing.
A larger sample simply means more urine was collected.
Your report did not include a reference range for urine sample volume, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Amount collected: This only records how much urine was in the container.
The sample volume does not show how much urine you make each day.
No action is needed for this item on its own.
This section lists any other findings the lab noted in your urine sample, such as mucus or sperm cells.
Labs record anything else they see under the microscope.
Most of these notes are minor, but the lab may flag something that needs a look.
The lab's method and reporting format for this item are not confirmed, so CURA does not label the result. Use the wording on your report and ask the lab or your doctor if it is unclear.
Sample collection: How the sample was collected changes what the lab sees.
Lab notes: These are free-text remarks, so their meaning depends on what was written.
What is noted here varies between labs and is not standardised.
Ask your doctor about anything listed here that is not explained elsewhere on your report.
Homocysteine is a substance your body makes when it breaks down protein. Vitamins B12, B6 and folate help clear it.
Homocysteine forms naturally when your body processes an amino acid called methionine.
B vitamins turn it into other useful substances.
When these vitamins are low, homocysteine can build up.
High homocysteine often points to low B12 or folate, and is linked with a higher risk of heart disease and blood clots.
A low homocysteine is not a concern.
Your homocysteine is inside the lab's range.

A higher homocysteine most often reflects low vitamin B12 or folate, which is common in vegetarian diets. Kidney problems, an underactive thyroid, smoking and some inherited patterns can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for homocysteine, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Vitamin B12 and folate levels: The body needs B12 and folate to break down homocysteine, so shortages raise it.
Vegetarian diet: Lower B12 intake in vegetarian diets often raises homocysteine.
Kidney function: The kidneys clear homocysteine, so kidney disease raises it.
Smoking: Smoking is linked with higher homocysteine.
Inherited patterns: Some people inherit slower homocysteine breakdown.
Some medicines: Metformin and some seizure medicines can raise it by lowering B12 or folate.
Lowering homocysteine has not been shown to reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke in most cases, though correcting a real B12 shortage still matters.
Lowering homocysteine with vitamins has not been shown to reduce heart disease in most studies. It is mainly a pointer to check B vitamins.
Enough B12 from dairy, eggs or fortified foods and folate from green leafy vegetables and dal help keep homocysteine down.
Eat leafy greens, dal and beans regularly. They are rich in folate, which helps clear homocysteine.
Include B12 sources such as milk, curd, eggs or fish, or B12-fortified foods if you are vegan.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Smoking raises homocysteine and harms blood vessels.
Folate from leafy greens, pulses and citrus, and B12 from dairy, eggs, fish or meat help keep homocysteine low.
Talk to a doctor if homocysteine is high, so they can check B12, folate and kidney function before any treatment.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein, or hs-CRP, measures small amounts of CRP, a protein your liver makes when there is inflammation in the body.
When your body is fighting infection or injury, the liver releases more CRP.
The high-sensitivity test picks up low levels linked with long-term, low-grade inflammation.
Low-grade inflammation in blood vessels plays a part in heart disease.
hs-CRP is used as one extra guide to heart risk, alongside cholesterol and blood pressure.
A low hs-CRP suggests little inflammation, which is favourable for heart health.
Your hs-CRP is inside the lab's range, suggesting no marked inflammation at the moment.

A higher hs-CRP can mean low-grade inflammation linked with higher heart risk. It also rises with any recent infection, injury, gum disease, extra weight or smoking, so a high value is usually repeated after a few weeks when you are well.
Your report did not include a reference range for high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Recent infection or injury: Any infection, even a cold, or an injury raises CRP for a few weeks.
Body weight: Body fat releases signals that keep CRP mildly raised.
Smoking: Smoking keeps inflammation raised.
Physical activity: Regular activity is linked with lower CRP.
Ongoing inflammatory conditions: Arthritis, gum disease and other long-term inflammation raise CRP.
A high hs-CRP after a recent cold does not reflect heart risk. Doctors repeat it when you are well.
hs-CRP shows inflammation but not where it is or why. A recent cold can raise it.
Regular activity, not smoking and a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains are linked with lower inflammation.
Stay active on most days, such as brisk walking. Regular activity is linked with lower inflammation.
Eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses, nuts and whole grains. These eating patterns are linked with lower CRP.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Smoking keeps inflammation raised.
Extra body fat, smoking, inactivity and poor sleep are linked with higher CRP. Regular activity and a diet with plenty of plant foods are linked with lower levels.
Talk to a doctor if hs-CRP stays high on a repeat test, or if it is very high, as that usually means an infection or inflammatory condition needs checking.

ESR, or erythrocyte (red blood cell) sedimentation rate, measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube of blood. It is a general sign of inflammation and is shown here as part of an inflammation panel.
During inflammation, the liver releases proteins that make red cells clump together.
Clumped cells are heavier and settle faster.
So ESR shows that inflammation may be present, but not where or why.
ESR is a simple check for inflammation and is used to follow some long-term inflammatory conditions.
A lower ESR is usually not a concern. Some conditions lower it, such as having too many red cells (polycythaemia), sickle cell anaemia or heart failure.
Your ESR is inside the lab's range, suggesting no marked inflammation from this test.

A higher ESR can come from infection, inflammation, autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, anaemia, pregnancy, kidney disease or thyroid disease. The normal upper limit is higher in older adults and in women.
Your report did not include a reference range for red cell settling rate (ESR), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Infection: Infection makes the liver release proteins that cause red cells to clump, so they settle faster.
Inflammation: Any inflammation raises these proteins and the ESR.
Age and sex: The normal upper limit is higher in older adults and in women.
Anaemia: With fewer red cells in the tube, the cells settle faster, raising ESR without inflammation.
Pregnancy: Pregnancy raises ESR.
Autoimmune conditions: Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus raise ESR.
Kidney disease: Kidney disease can raise ESR.
Thyroid disease: Thyroid disease can raise ESR.
Red cell and heart conditions: Too many red cells (polycythaemia), sickle cell anaemia and heart failure lower ESR.
A normal ESR does not rule out inflammation, and a raised ESR does not show where it is. CRP is often checked alongside it.
ESR is non-specific. A normal ESR does not rule out inflammation, and a raised ESR does not show the cause.
Talk to a doctor if ESR is high, especially with unexplained fever, joint pain, muscle symptoms or a new headache.
Testosterone is a sex hormone made mainly in the testes in men and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands in women. Total testosterone measures all of it in your blood.
In men, testosterone supports sex drive, sperm production, muscle, bone strength and energy.
In women, smaller amounts support sex drive, bone and muscle.
Levels are highest in the morning and fall gradually with age in men.
Total testosterone helps check for low testosterone in men and for high androgen levels in women, which can be part of PCOS.

In men, a lower testosterone can come from ageing, extra weight, poor sleep, long illness, some medicines or problems with the testes or pituitary gland. It can cause low sex drive, tiredness and loss of muscle.
Your testosterone is inside the lab's range for the reference group used.

In women, a higher testosterone often goes with PCOS and can cause irregular periods, acne or extra hair growth. In men, high levels are uncommon and can come from testosterone or anabolic steroid use.
Your report did not include a reference range for total testosterone, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Time of day: Testosterone is highest in the morning, so a later sample reads lower.
Age and sex: Men have much higher levels than women, and men's levels fall slowly with age.
Body weight: Extra body fat converts testosterone to oestrogen and lowers it in men.
Sleep: Poor or short sleep lowers testosterone in men.
PCOS: In women, polycystic ovary syndrome raises testosterone, causing acne, extra hair and irregular periods.
Testosterone or steroid use: Taking testosterone or anabolic steroids raises the level and stops the body's own production.
Low energy in men is not always low testosterone. Sleep, mood, thyroid and anaemia are common causes too.
Testosterone varies by time of day and is best checked in the morning. A low result is usually repeated before any diagnosis.
Enough sleep, regular activity including strength exercise, and a healthy weight support normal testosterone in men.
Aim for 7 to 8 hours of sleep. Testosterone is made mostly during sleep.
Stay active and include some strength exercise. It supports muscle and a healthy weight, which helps hormone balance.
Extra body weight, poor sleep and heavy alcohol use are linked with lower testosterone in men.
Men: talk to a doctor if testosterone is low and you have low sex drive, erection problems or tiredness.
Women: talk to a doctor if testosterone is high and you have irregular periods, acne or extra hair growth.
DHEA-S is a hormone made mainly by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of your kidneys. Your body can turn it into other sex hormones.
The adrenal glands make DHEA-S in large amounts in young adults.
DHEA-S is a building block for testosterone and oestrogen.
Levels fall naturally as you age.
DHEA-S helps check whether extra male-type hormones are coming from the adrenal glands, for example in women with acne or extra hair growth.
A lower DHEA-S is common with ageing. It can also be seen with adrenal or pituitary problems or long-term steroid medicines.
Your DHEA-S is inside the lab's range for your age and sex.
A higher DHEA-S can be seen with PCOS or, less often, with adrenal gland conditions. In women it can cause acne, extra hair growth or irregular periods.
Your report did not include a reference range for DHEA-S (adrenal hormone), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Age: DHEA-S peaks in young adulthood and falls steadily with age.
Sex: Men have higher levels than women.
PCOS: Some women with PCOS have higher DHEA-S from the adrenal glands.
Adrenal conditions: Adrenal growths or inherited adrenal conditions raise it; adrenal failure lowers it.
Steroid medicines: Steroid tablets switch off adrenal production and lower DHEA-S.
DHEA supplements are not proven to slow ageing, and they can raise testosterone in women.
Normal ranges change a lot with age, so the result must be read against the right age group.
Talk to a doctor if DHEA-S is high with acne, extra hair growth or irregular periods, or if it is very high.
IGF-1 is a hormone made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone. It reflects how much growth hormone your body has been making.
Growth hormone from the pituitary gland tells the liver to make IGF-1.
IGF-1 helps build bone and muscle and repair tissue.
Levels peak in the teenage years and fall with age.
IGF-1 is used to check for too much or too little growth hormone.
A lower IGF-1 can come from ageing, poor nutrition, liver disease, an underactive thyroid, poorly controlled diabetes or low growth hormone.
Your IGF-1 is inside the lab's range for your age.
A higher IGF-1 can be seen in puberty and pregnancy. Persistently high levels in adults can, rarely, mean the pituitary is making too much growth hormone.
Your report did not include a reference range for IGF-1 (growth-related hormone), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Age: IGF-1 is highest in teenage years and falls with age, so ranges are age-specific.
Nutrition: Undernutrition lowers IGF-1.
Liver function: The liver makes IGF-1, so liver disease lowers it.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid lowers IGF-1.
Pituitary activity: Too much growth hormone from the pituitary raises IGF-1; too little lowers it.
IGF-1 is only meaningful against an age-matched range.
IGF-1 ranges depend strongly on age, and results differ between labs.
Very low calorie or protein intake can lower IGF-1.
Talk to a doctor if IGF-1 is outside the range for your age, especially with changes in hand or foot size, facial features, or unexplained tiredness.
Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands. It helps your body respond to stress, control blood sugar and blood pressure, and regulate your sleep and wake cycle.
Cortisol is highest in the early morning and lowest around midnight.
Cortisol rises during physical or emotional stress.
The brain controls how much cortisol the adrenal glands release.
Cortisol is used to check whether the adrenal glands are making too much or too little.

A lower cortisol can be normal if the sample was taken later in the day. A low morning cortisol can point to adrenal insufficiency, where the glands do not make enough, or follow stopping steroid medicines.
Your cortisol is inside the lab's range for the time the sample was taken.

A higher cortisol can come from stress, illness, poor sleep, pregnancy, hormone pills or steroid medicines. Rarely, it is due to Cushing syndrome, where the body makes too much cortisol for a long time.
Your report did not include a reference range for cortisol (stress-response hormone), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Time of day: Cortisol is highest early in the morning and lowest around midnight, so timing changes the result a great deal.
Stress and illness: Physical illness and severe stress raise cortisol.
Sleep: Night shifts and poor sleep shift the daily pattern.
Steroid medicines: Steroid tablets, creams and inhalers lower the body's own cortisol, while some lab methods read prednisolone as cortisol.
Hormone pills or pregnancy: Oestrogen raises the protein that carries cortisol, raising total cortisol.
A single cortisol result cannot diagnose stress or adrenal fatigue. Adrenal fatigue is not a recognised medical condition.
A single cortisol result depends heavily on the time of day. Special timed tests are needed to diagnose adrenal conditions.
Regular sleep at similar times supports a normal daily cortisol rhythm.
Keep a regular sleep and wake time. Cortisol follows a daily rhythm that steady sleep helps support.
Make time for things that help you unwind, such as walking, prayer, breathing exercises or time with friends. These can ease the stress response.
Ongoing stress and poor sleep can change cortisol patterns.

Talk to a doctor if cortisol is clearly abnormal, especially with weight gain around the tummy, purple stretch marks, or with weakness, dizziness, weight loss and salt cravings. Never stop steroid medicines suddenly.
Parathyroid hormone, or PTH, is made by four tiny glands in your neck. It controls the calcium level in your blood.
When blood calcium falls, PTH rises.
PTH releases calcium from bones, helps kidneys keep calcium and activates vitamin D to absorb more from food.
When calcium is high, PTH should fall.
PTH is read with calcium and vitamin D to find the cause of calcium problems.
A lower PTH with high calcium suggests the calcium rise is coming from somewhere else. Low PTH with low calcium can mean the parathyroid glands are underactive, for example after neck surgery.
Your PTH is inside the lab's range. It is interpreted together with calcium.
A higher PTH with high calcium usually points to an overactive parathyroid gland. A higher PTH with normal or low calcium often means low vitamin D or kidney disease.
Your report did not include a reference range for parathyroid hormone (PTH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Calcium level: When blood calcium falls, the parathyroid glands release more PTH to raise it.
Vitamin D level: Low vitamin D lowers calcium absorption, so PTH rises to compensate.
Kidney function: Kidney disease upsets calcium and phosphate and raises PTH.
Magnesium level: Very low magnesium stops the glands releasing PTH.
A high PTH with low vitamin D often settles once vitamin D is corrected, rather than meaning a gland problem.
PTH cannot be interpreted without a calcium result taken at the same time.
Enough vitamin D and calcium from food support normal PTH.
Spend some time in daylight and include calcium and vitamin D foods. Low vitamin D is a common reason PTH rises.
Low vitamin D, from little sunlight or diet, is a common reason PTH rises.
Talk to a doctor if PTH is abnormal together with abnormal calcium, kidney stones, bone pain or thinning bones.
Prolactin is a hormone made by the pituitary gland in your brain. Its main job is to help make breast milk after childbirth.
Prolactin rises in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Prolactin also affects periods and fertility in women and sex drive in men.
Stress, sleep and some medicines can raise it.
High prolactin can cause irregular or missed periods, milk leakage, low sex drive and fertility problems.
A low prolactin is rarely a concern.
Your prolactin is inside the lab's range.

A higher prolactin can come from pregnancy, breastfeeding, stress, a recent meal or exercise, an underactive thyroid, kidney disease or some medicines such as certain anti-sickness and mental health medicines. A small harmless growth on the pituitary called a prolactinoma is another cause.
Your report did not include a reference range for prolactin, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Prolactin rises naturally to make breast milk.
Stress: Physical stress, including a difficult blood draw, can raise prolactin.
Some medicines: Some antipsychotic, anti-sickness and acid medicines raise prolactin.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid raises prolactin.
Kidney function: Kidney disease reduces prolactin clearance.
Time of sample: Prolactin is higher during sleep and early morning.
A mildly high prolactin is often from stress or medicines and is usually rechecked before further tests.
Mildly high prolactin is often repeated, as stress or the blood draw itself can raise it.
Talk to a doctor if prolactin is high, especially with missed periods, milk from the breasts when not breastfeeding, headaches or vision changes.
Luteinising hormone, or LH, is made by the pituitary gland. It signals the ovaries to release an egg and the testes to make testosterone.
In women, LH rises sharply in the middle of the cycle to trigger ovulation.
In men, LH tells the testes to make testosterone.
After menopause, LH rises because the ovaries stop responding.
LH helps check fertility, periods, menopause and testosterone problems. In some women with PCOS, LH is higher compared with FSH.
A lower LH can mean the pituitary is not sending enough signal. It can also be seen with hormone pills, stress, very low body weight or heavy exercise.
Your LH is inside the lab's range for the reference group used.
A higher LH can be normal mid-cycle or after menopause. Outside these times, it can be seen with PCOS or when the ovaries or testes are not working well.
Your report did not include a reference range for luteinising hormone (LH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Menstrual cycle day: LH surges in mid-cycle to trigger ovulation, so results depend on the day.
Menopause: After menopause the ovaries stop responding and LH rises.
Hormone pills: Contraceptive pills lower LH.
PCOS: Many women with PCOS have LH higher than FSH.
Body weight and exercise: Very low weight or heavy training lowers LH and can stop periods.
An LH result means little without knowing the cycle day.
LH in women must be read against the day of the menstrual cycle the sample was taken.
Very low body weight, intense exercise and severe stress can lower LH.
Talk to a doctor if LH is abnormal along with irregular or missed periods, difficulty getting pregnant, or low testosterone symptoms.
Follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, is made by the pituitary gland. It helps eggs develop in the ovaries and sperm develop in the testes.
In women, FSH helps egg follicles grow early in each cycle.
In men, it supports sperm production.
FSH rises around menopause as the ovaries respond less.
FSH helps check fertility, menopause and the function of the ovaries and testes.
A lower FSH can mean the pituitary is not sending enough signal, or can be seen with hormone pills, pregnancy, very low body weight or stress.
Your FSH is inside the lab's range for the reference group used.
A higher FSH in women often goes with menopause or reduced ovarian reserve. In men, it can mean the testes are not making sperm well.
Your report did not include a reference range for follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Menstrual cycle day: FSH rises early in the cycle to grow egg follicles.
Menopause: FSH rises as the ovaries run low on eggs.
Age: FSH rises gradually as fertility falls with age.
Hormone pills: Contraceptive pills lower FSH.
Body weight: Very low body weight lowers FSH.
A single FSH cannot confirm menopause in women who still have periods; levels swing from month to month.
FSH in women varies through the cycle and is usually checked in the first few days of a period.
Talk to a doctor if FSH is abnormal along with irregular or missed periods, difficulty getting pregnant, or hot flushes before 40.
This result measures calcium, the mineral that keeps bones strong and helps muscles, nerves and the heart work. The lab has not confirmed whether it is total or free (ionised) calcium.
Most calcium is stored in bones.
A small amount in blood is carefully controlled by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D.
Free calcium is the active part; total calcium includes calcium carried on albumin.
Calcium helps check bone health, parathyroid function, vitamin D status and kidney function.
A lower calcium can come from low vitamin D, low albumin, low magnesium, kidney disease or low parathyroid hormone.
Your calcium is inside the lab's range.
A higher calcium most often comes from an overactive parathyroid gland, too much vitamin D or calcium from supplements, or dehydration.
Your report did not include a reference range for calcium (assay unconfirmed), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Which calcium was measured: The lab has not confirmed whether this is total or ionised calcium, which have different ranges.
Vitamin D: Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium.
Parathyroid hormone: This hormone raises blood calcium.
Albumin: Low albumin lowers total calcium without a true shortage.
Kidney function: Kidneys help balance calcium.
Supplements: Large doses of vitamin D or calcium can push it high.
Blood calcium does not show bone strength.
The lab has not confirmed whether this is total or free calcium, so this result should not be compared directly with the total calcium result on your report.
Calcium from milk, curd, ragi and sesame, with enough vitamin D, supports bones.
Include calcium foods such as milk, curd, ragi, sesame or calcium-set tofu. These support bone health.
Dietary calcium and vitamin D support bones, though blood calcium rarely changes with diet alone.
Talk to a doctor if calcium is abnormal, especially with cramps, tingling, extreme thirst, confusion or kidney stones.
PSA, or prostate-specific antigen, is a protein made by the prostate gland, a small gland below the bladder in men.
The prostate makes PSA to help semen stay liquid.
A small amount enters the blood.
PSA tends to rise with age as the prostate grows.
This marker is mainly used to follow people already being treated for certain cancers, and sometimes to help investigate symptoms.
A low result is expected and is not a concern.
Your PSA is inside the lab's range. A normal PSA lowers the likelihood of significant prostate cancer but does not rule it out.

A higher PSA is most often due to a larger prostate with age, prostate inflammation or infection, recent ejaculation, cycling or a recent urinary procedure. Prostate cancer is one possible cause and needs further checks.
Your report did not include a reference range for prostate-specific antigen (PSA), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Age: PSA rises as the prostate grows with age, so normal levels are higher in older men.
Prostate enlargement: A benign enlarged prostate, common after 50, raises PSA.
Prostate inflammation or infection: Prostatitis can raise PSA sharply for weeks.
Recent ejaculation or cycling: Both can raise PSA a little for a day or two.
Some medicines: Medicines for an enlarged prostate, such as finasteride, roughly halve PSA.
A high PSA does not mean cancer. Most raised PSA results come from enlargement or inflammation.
This marker is not a cancer screening test on its own. Many non-cancer conditions raise it, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
PSA screening has benefits and harms. Decisions about testing are best made with a doctor.
Talk to a doctor about any raised result, so it can be put in context and, if needed, repeated or followed up with other tests. Most raised results are not caused by cancer.
CEA, or carcinoembryonic antigen, is a protein that is normally present only in very small amounts in adult blood.
Some cells, especially in the bowel, make CEA.
Levels can rise with some cancers, but also with smoking and inflammation.
This marker is mainly used to follow people already being treated for certain cancers, and sometimes to help investigate symptoms.
A low result is expected and is not a concern.
Your CEA is inside the lab's range.
A higher CEA can come from smoking, inflammation of the bowel, liver or lungs, or pancreatitis. Some cancers, especially bowel cancer, can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Smoking: Smokers have higher CEA.
Inflammatory bowel conditions: Gut inflammation raises CEA.
Liver disease: The liver clears CEA, so liver disease raises it.
Lung conditions: Some lung conditions raise CEA.
Some cancers: Some bowel and other cancers make CEA, which is why it is used to follow treatment.
Tumour markers are not cancer screening tests for most people. Many non-cancer conditions raise them, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
This marker is not a cancer screening test on its own. Many non-cancer conditions raise it, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
Smokers often have higher CEA than non-smokers.
Talk to a doctor about any raised result, so it can be put in context and, if needed, repeated or followed up with other tests. Most raised results are not caused by cancer.

AFP, or alpha-fetoprotein, is a protein made by a developing baby and, in adults, in small amounts by the liver. The report labels this as an amniotic fluid test, so the lab needs to confirm which sample was used.
In pregnancy, AFP passes from the baby into the mother's blood and the fluid around the baby.
In adults, high blood AFP can be linked with some liver conditions and some cancers.
AFP in pregnancy screens for some birth conditions. In adults, it is used to follow some liver and testicular cancers.
The sample type for this AFP result is not confirmed, so CURA does not interpret it. Ask the lab or your doctor which sample was tested.
Sample type: The lab has not confirmed whether this was blood or another fluid, which changes its meaning.
Pregnancy: The baby makes AFP, so levels rise in pregnancy.
Liver conditions: Hepatitis and cirrhosis can raise AFP.
Tumour markers are not cancer screening tests for most people. Many non-cancer conditions raise them, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
Amniotic fluid AFP and adult blood AFP have completely different purposes and ranges, so this result cannot be interpreted until the sample is confirmed.
Ask your doctor or the lab what sample this AFP result came from before reading anything into it.
CA 19-9 is a protein found on some cells of the pancreas, bile ducts and gut. It is mainly used to follow pancreatic and bile duct conditions.
Small amounts are normal in the blood.
CA 19-9 rises when bile flow is blocked or the pancreas is inflamed, as well as with some cancers.
This marker is mainly used to follow people already being treated for certain cancers, and sometimes to help investigate symptoms.
A low result is expected and is not a concern.
Your CA 19-9 is inside the lab's range.
A higher CA 19-9 is often caused by blocked bile flow, gallstones, pancreatitis, liver conditions or diabetes. Some cancers of the pancreas and bile ducts can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for CA 19-9, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Bile duct blockage: Blocked bile flow raises CA 19-9, sometimes to very high levels.
Pancreatitis: Pancreas inflammation raises it.
Liver conditions: Liver disease raises it.
Diabetes: Poorly controlled diabetes can raise it.
Some cancers: Some pancreas and bile duct cancers make it.
Tumour markers are not cancer screening tests for most people. Many non-cancer conditions raise them, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
This marker is not a cancer screening test on its own. Many non-cancer conditions raise it, and a normal result does not rule out cancer.
Some people cannot make CA 19-9 because of their blood group genes, so their level stays low even with disease.
Talk to a doctor about any raised result, so it can be put in context and, if needed, repeated or followed up with other tests. Most raised results are not caused by cancer.
CA 125 is a protein found on some cells, including those lining the ovaries, womb, tummy and chest. It is mainly used to follow ovarian conditions.
Small amounts are normal in the blood.
CA 125 can rise with many conditions that irritate these linings.
This marker is mainly used to follow people already being treated for certain cancers, and sometimes to help investigate symptoms.
A low result is expected and is not a concern.
Your CA 125 is inside the lab's range.
A higher CA 125 is often caused by periods, pregnancy, endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, liver disease or fluid in the tummy. Ovarian cancer is one possible cause.

Menstrual cycle: CA 125 can rise during periods.
Pregnancy: It rises in early pregnancy.

Pelvic infection: Infection of the pelvic organs raises it.

Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a type of cholesterol-carrying particle whose level is set mostly by the genes you inherit.
Lp(a) looks like an LDL particle with an extra protein attached.
Lipoprotein(a) can add to plaque build-up in arteries and may make blood clots more likely.
Your level stays fairly steady through life because it is mainly inherited.
A high Lp(a) can raise heart and stroke risk even when other cholesterol results look fine.
Many experts suggest checking it at least once in adulthood, especially with early heart disease in the family.
A low Lp(a) means this inherited risk factor is not raised.
Your Lp(a) is inside the lab's range, so this inherited risk factor does not appear to be raised.
A higher Lp(a) means an inherited increase in heart and blood vessel risk. It does not mean you have heart disease, but it makes managing your other risk factors more important.
Your report did not include a reference range for Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Inherited genes: Lp(a) is set mostly by genes, so it stays roughly the same through life.
Kidney disease: Some kidney conditions can raise Lp(a).
Menopause: Lp(a) can rise somewhat after menopause.
Some medicines: A few medicines change Lp(a) a little; ordinary statins usually do not lower it.
Labs often use fixed risk cut-offs for Lp(a), such as above 50 mg/dL or 125 nmol/L, and the units differ between labs, so compare with the cut-off printed on your report.
A high Lp(a) is not something you caused by eating badly. It is mainly inherited.
Different labs report Lp(a) in different units, so results from different labs cannot always be compared directly.
Diet and exercise do not change Lp(a) much, so a high result is a reason to control the risks you can change: LDL, blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking.
Because it is inherited, close family members may want their Lp(a) checked.
Lp(a) is mostly decided by genes and changes very little with diet or exercise.
Talk to a doctor if Lp(a) is high. They may focus more closely on your LDL, blood pressure and other risks.
Close family members may want to ask about being tested, as high Lp(a) runs in families.
Apolipoprotein B, or ApoB, is a protein found on each particle that can carry cholesterol into artery walls. Measuring it gives a count of those particles.
Each LDL, VLDL and Lp(a) particle carries one ApoB protein.
So ApoB shows how many plaque-forming particles are in your blood, not just how much cholesterol they hold.
More particles means more chances for them to get trapped in artery walls.
ApoB can show raised heart risk that LDL misses, especially in people with high triglycerides, diabetes or extra weight.
A lower ApoB means fewer plaque-forming particles, which is generally favourable.
Your ApoB is inside the lab's range, suggesting the number of plaque-forming particles is not raised.
A higher ApoB means more cholesterol-carrying particles that can build up in arteries. It is linked with higher heart risk, even if LDL looks acceptable.
Your report did not include a reference range for apolipoprotein B (ApoB), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Inherited patterns: Genes set how many cholesterol-carrying particles your liver releases and clears.
Triglyceride levels: High triglycerides often come with many small particles, each carrying one ApoB, so ApoB can be high even when LDL looks moderate.
Diet and body weight: Saturated fat, sugar and extra weight increase the number of these particles.
Insulin resistance or diabetes: Poor insulin action raises the number of small, dense particles.
Cholesterol-lowering medicines: Statins lower ApoB along with LDL.

Many labs print a desirable cut-off rather than a range drawn from healthy people. The level a doctor aims for depends on your overall heart risk, including blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, so the same number can be fine for one person and too high for another.
ApoB is not another kind of cholesterol. It counts the particles that can enter artery walls, so it can add information when LDL and triglycerides disagree.
ApoB is not part of every routine cholesterol test, and target levels depend on your overall heart risk.
Keep doing what supports your blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, and meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts.
Cholesterol can change over years with weight, age and menopause, so repeat checks at the interval your doctor suggests matter even when this result is good.
Blood pressure, blood sugar and smoking add to the same artery risk as cholesterol, so working on any of them protects your heart.
If close family members had heart disease young, tell your doctor. It changes how your results are judged.
Choose plant oils, dal, beans and vegetables more often than fried foods and fatty meat. This lowers the cholesterol particles that ApoB counts.
Cut back on sugary foods and drinks. Extra sugar makes the liver release more fat-carrying particles.
Stay active on most days. Activity helps your body clear blood fats.
The habits that lower LDL and triglycerides, such as less saturated fat and sugar, more fibre and regular activity, also tend to lower ApoB.
Talk to a doctor if ApoB is high, especially alongside diabetes, high blood pressure or early heart disease in your family.
Serum iron measures the iron travelling in your blood right now. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
Iron from food is absorbed in the gut.
Iron travels in the blood attached to a carrier protein called transferrin.
Spare iron is stored as ferritin, mainly in the liver.
Serum iron is read with ferritin, TIBC and transferrin saturation to check for low iron or too much iron.
Lower serum iron can come from low iron stores, blood loss, low iron intake, or inflammation, which hides iron away from the blood.
Your serum iron is inside the lab's range. It is read together with ferritin to judge your stores.
Higher serum iron can follow iron tablets or a recent iron-rich meal. It can also be seen with iron overload conditions or liver damage.
Your report did not include a reference range for serum iron, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron intake and tablets: Iron tablets or an iron-rich meal raise blood iron for several hours.
Time of day: Iron is highest in the morning and lower later in the day.
Recent meals: Eating before the test can raise the result.
Blood loss: Losing blood uses up iron.
Inflammation: During inflammation the body locks iron away, so blood iron falls even if stores are fine.
Serum iron changes hour to hour, so ferritin is a better guide to stores.
Serum iron changes through the day and after meals, so it is not reliable on its own.
Iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, eggs, fish or meat, eaten with a vitamin C food such as lemon, amla or guava, help keep iron stores up.
Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption, so having them an hour away from meals helps.
Heavy periods are the most common reason Indian women run low on iron. If periods are heavy, tell your doctor.
Include iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, jaggery in moderation, eggs, fish or meat. Your body needs iron to make haemoglobin.
Have a vitamin C food with iron-rich meals, such as lemon, amla, guava or tomato. Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods.
Keep tea and coffee away from meals by about an hour. They reduce how much iron you absorb.
Iron-rich foods, with vitamin C, help keep iron levels up. Tea and coffee with meals reduce absorption.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are low, so they can find the cause, such as heavy periods or blood loss from the gut, before starting tablets.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are high, as iron overload can harm the liver and heart.
TIBC, or total iron-binding capacity, measures how much iron your blood could carry if all its carrier protein were full.
Iron travels in the blood on a protein called transferrin.
When iron stores are low, the liver makes more transferrin, so TIBC rises.
TIBC helps tell low iron apart from other causes of anaemia.
A lower TIBC can be seen with inflammation, long-term illness, liver disease, poor nutrition or iron overload.
Your TIBC is inside the lab's range.
A higher TIBC usually means your body is short of iron and is making more carrier protein to capture it. It can also rise in pregnancy or with hormone pills.
Your report did not include a reference range for total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron stores: When stores are low, the liver makes more transferrin to catch iron, so TIBC rises.
Inflammation: Inflammation lowers TIBC.
Pregnancy or hormone pills: Oestrogen raises transferrin and TIBC.
Liver function: The liver makes transferrin, so liver disease lowers TIBC.
Nutrition: Poor nutrition lowers TIBC.
A high TIBC is not too much iron. It usually means the body is hungry for iron.
TIBC is read together with serum iron and ferritin; on its own it cannot confirm low iron.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are low, so they can find the cause, such as heavy periods or blood loss from the gut, before starting tablets.
UIBC, or unsaturated iron-binding capacity, measures how much spare room is left on the iron carrier protein in your blood.
Iron travels on a protein called transferrin.
UIBC is the part of that carrier that is still empty.
UIBC is used to work out TIBC and transferrin saturation.
A lower UIBC means less empty carrier space, which can be seen with high iron or with inflammation.
Your UIBC is inside the lab's range.
A higher UIBC means more empty carrier space, which usually points to low iron.
Your report did not include a reference range for unused iron-binding capacity (UIBC), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: Less iron in the blood leaves more carrier spaces empty, raising UIBC.
Transferrin level: More carrier protein, as in iron shortage or pregnancy, raises UIBC.
Inflammation: Inflammation lowers transferrin and UIBC.
UIBC adds little on its own; it is read with iron and TIBC.
UIBC is mostly a step in calculating other iron results and is rarely read on its own.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are low, so they can find the cause, such as heavy periods or blood loss from the gut, before starting tablets.
Transferrin saturation shows what percentage of the iron carrier protein in your blood is filled with iron.
Transferrin carries iron around your body.
This result is worked out by dividing serum iron by TIBC.
A low saturation suggests low iron, while a high saturation can be an early sign of iron overload.
A lower saturation means the carrier holds little iron, which usually points to low iron.
Your transferrin saturation is inside the lab's range.
A higher saturation means a lot of the carrier is full. It can follow iron tablets, but a persistently high result can point to iron overload, such as haemochromatosis, an inherited condition.
Your report did not include a reference range for transferrin saturation, so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron level: Saturation falls as blood iron falls.
Iron tablets: Recent iron tablets raise saturation for some hours.
Inherited iron overload: Haemochromatosis makes the gut absorb too much iron, raising saturation.
Inflammation: Inflammation lowers blood iron and saturation.
A high saturation is worth checking even if you feel well, because iron overload can quietly damage the liver and heart.
Transferrin saturation varies through the day, so a high result is usually repeated on a fasting sample.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are low, so they can find the cause, such as heavy periods or blood loss from the gut, before starting tablets.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are high, as iron overload can harm the liver and heart.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron inside your body. The amount in your blood reflects how much iron you have in reserve.
Your body keeps spare iron in ferritin, mostly in the liver.
When you need more iron to make red blood cells, it is released from these stores.
Low ferritin is usually the earliest sign that iron is running low.
Ferritin is the best single blood test for low iron stores.
Lower ferritin means your iron stores are low. Common causes are heavy periods, pregnancy, low iron intake, blood loss from the gut or poor absorption.
Your ferritin is inside the lab's range, suggesting adequate iron stores at the moment.

Higher ferritin can come from inflammation, infection, liver strain such as fatty liver, heavy alcohol use or iron overload. Because inflammation raises ferritin, a high level does not always mean too much iron.
Your report did not include a reference range for ferritin (stored iron), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Iron intake: Too little iron from food slowly empties stores.
Heavy periods or blood loss: Regular blood loss is the most common reason stores run low.
Pregnancy: The baby draws on the mother's stores.
Inflammation: Ferritin rises during inflammation, so it can look normal or high even when stores are low.
Liver health: Fatty liver and other liver strain raise ferritin.
Alcohol: Regular drinking raises ferritin.
Many labs print a lower limit for ferritin that is lower than the level doctors use to diagnose iron deficiency, so a result at the bottom of the range can still mean low stores.
A high ferritin does not always mean too much iron. Inflammation, liver disease, obesity and alcohol can also raise it.
Inflammation can raise ferritin and hide low iron stores, so a normal ferritin during illness does not always rule out low iron.
Iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, eggs, fish or meat, eaten with a vitamin C food such as lemon, amla or guava, help keep iron stores up.
Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption, so having them an hour away from meals helps.
Heavy periods are the most common reason Indian women run low on iron. If periods are heavy, tell your doctor.
Include iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, rajma, green leafy vegetables, jaggery in moderation, eggs, fish or meat. Your body needs iron to make haemoglobin.
Have a vitamin C food with iron-rich meals, such as lemon, amla, guava or tomato. Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods.
Keep tea and coffee away from meals by about an hour. They reduce how much iron you absorb.
Iron-rich foods with vitamin C help build stores. Vegetarian diets can provide enough iron with planning.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are low, so they can find the cause, such as heavy periods or blood loss from the gut, before starting tablets.
Talk to a doctor if iron results are high, as iron overload can harm the liver and heart.
Creatine kinase, or CK, is an enzyme found mainly in your muscles, including the heart. It leaks into the blood when muscles are strained or damaged.
Muscles use CK to make energy quickly.
After hard exercise or an injury, some CK passes into the blood.
People with more muscle naturally have higher CK.
CK helps check for muscle damage, including side effects of some medicines such as statins.
A low CK is usually not a concern and often reflects less muscle.
Your CK is inside the lab's range, suggesting no sign of muscle strain from this test.
A higher CK most often follows hard or unfamiliar exercise, a fall or injury, or an injection into muscle. It can also be raised by some medicines, an underactive thyroid or muscle conditions.
Your report did not include a reference range for creatine kinase (CK), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Recent exercise: Hard or unaccustomed exercise causes small muscle injuries that release CK for several days.
Muscle injury: Injured muscle, for example after a fall or a crush injury, releases CK.
Muscle mass: People with more muscle have higher normal levels.
Statins and some other medicines: Statins can occasionally irritate muscles and raise CK, especially with muscle pain.
Thyroid function: An underactive thyroid can raise CK.
A high CK after a heavy workout is common and settles. It is the combination with muscle pain, weakness or dark urine that needs urgent care.
CK does not show which muscle is affected. Heart muscle damage is checked with different tests.
Avoid very hard workouts for two to three days before a repeat test. Exercise raises CK and can hide the real picture.
Heavy or new exercise in the days before the test can raise CK for up to a week.
See a doctor promptly if CK is high with muscle pain or weakness, dark or cola-coloured urine, or if you take a statin and develop muscle aches.
Lactate dehydrogenase, or LDH, is an enzyme found in almost every tissue in your body. It rises in the blood when cells are damaged.
LDH helps cells turn sugar into energy.
LDH is found in the heart, liver, muscles, kidneys, lungs and blood cells.
When cells are injured, LDH leaks out.
LDH is a general sign of tissue damage and is sometimes used to follow certain conditions.
A low LDH is not a concern.
Your LDH is inside the lab's range.

A higher LDH means some tissue damage somewhere, for example from muscle injury, hard exercise, liver problems, red blood cell breakdown, infection or, less often, some cancers. A falsely high value is common if red cells burst during sampling.
Your report did not include a reference range for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Tissue injury: LDH sits in almost every cell, so damage to any tissue releases it.
Hard exercise: Strenuous exercise can raise LDH for a while.
Red blood cell breakdown: Red cells contain LDH, so faster breakdown raises it.
Sample handling: If cells burst in the tube, LDH reads falsely high.
Liver conditions: Liver damage can raise LDH.
A raised LDH does not point to one organ. It shows that some tissue damage may be present and needs other tests to place it.
LDH is non-specific and cannot show which tissue is affected.
Talk to a doctor if LDH is high, especially with other abnormal results, tiredness, yellow eyes or unexplained weight loss.
Total IgE measures the overall amount of immunoglobulin E (IgE), a type of antibody involved in allergies, in your blood. It does not show what you are allergic to.
Antibodies are proteins your immune system makes to recognise threats.
IgE is the antibody type that triggers allergy symptoms like sneezing, itching and wheezing.
IgE also helps fight some parasites.
Total IgE can support a picture of allergic conditions, but specific allergy tests are needed to find triggers.
A low or normal total IgE does not rule out allergy to a particular substance.
Your total IgE is inside the lab's range. You can still be allergic to specific things.
A higher total IgE is common with allergies, asthma, eczema and hay fever. Parasite infections and, less often, some immune conditions can also raise it.
Your report did not include a reference range for total immunoglobulin E (IgE), so CURA cannot say whether it is high or low.
Allergic conditions: Asthma, eczema, hay fever and food allergy make the immune system produce more IgE.
Parasite infections: Worm infections, common in India, strongly raise total IgE.
Age: IgE is higher in childhood and tends to fall with age.
Some immune conditions: Rare immune conditions can raise IgE a great deal.
A normal total IgE does not rule out allergy, and a high one does not tell you what you are allergic to.
Total IgE cannot identify a specific allergen, and normal levels do not rule out allergy.
Keep a simple diary of symptoms and possible triggers, such as dust, pollen, pets or foods. It helps a doctor decide which specific tests are worth doing.
See a doctor about persistent sneezing, wheezing, rashes or reactions to food. Seek emergency care for swelling of the lips or throat, trouble breathing or fainting.

Dried pigeon droppings, common on balconies, window ledges and air-conditioner units in cities. This test looks for IgE, the allergy antibody, against it. It shows whether your immune system recognises it, not whether you are allergic.
Your immune system protects you by making antibodies, proteins that recognise things it sees as a threat.
In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
This test can help a doctor decide whether Pigeon Droppings might be linked to symptoms such as sneezing, itchy eyes, wheezing or skin rashes around animals or birds.

The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Pigeon Droppings. It does not prove you will react to it.
Antibodies to Pigeon Droppings were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
Little or no antibody to Pigeon Droppings was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.
An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.
If symptoms happen around animals or birds, keep them out of the bedroom and wash your hands after handling them.
Clean areas where birds roost or animals sleep regularly, and avoid stirring up dry droppings.
Animal and bird allergens collect in dust, bedding, furniture and clothes, even after the animal has left.
Talk to a doctor if you get symptoms around animals or birds, or ongoing breathlessness or cough.
Seek emergency care straight away for swelling of the face, eyes or tongue, a hoarse or whispered voice, trouble breathing or wheezing, dizziness or collapse after contact with any trigger.

A penicillin antibiotic given by injection. This test looks for IgE, the allergy antibody, against it. It shows whether your immune system recognises it, not whether you are allergic.
Your immune system protects you by making antibodies, proteins that recognise things it sees as a threat.
In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
This test may help a doctor or allergy specialist look into a past reaction to Penicillin G. For most medicines, blood tests are less reliable than a careful history and specialist testing.

The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Penicillin G. It does not prove you will react to it.

Little or no antibody to Penicillin G was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.

A penicillin antibiotic given by mouth or injection. This test looks for IgE, the allergy antibody, against it. It shows whether your immune system recognises it, not whether you are allergic.
Your immune system protects you by making antibodies, proteins that recognise things it sees as a threat.
In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
This test may help a doctor or allergy specialist look into a past reaction to Ampicillin. For most medicines, blood tests are less reliable than a careful history and specialist testing.

The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Ampicillin. It does not prove you will react to it.
Antibodies to Ampicillin were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
Little or no antibody to Ampicillin was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.
An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.
Keep a written list of any medicine that caused a reaction, what happened and when, and show it to every doctor and pharmacist.
Do not take a medicine you reacted to before, or stop a prescribed medicine, based on this result alone. Ask a doctor first.
Seek emergency care straight away for swelling of the face, eyes or tongue, a hoarse or whispered voice, trouble breathing or wheezing, dizziness or collapse after contact with any trigger.

In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
This test can help a doctor decide whether Cladosporium Herbarum, a type of mould or yeast, might be linked to nose, eye, chest or skin symptoms.

The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Cladosporium Herbarum. It does not prove you will react to it.
Antibodies to Cladosporium Herbarum were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
Little or no antibody to Cladosporium Herbarum was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.
An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.

Walnut (akhrot), a tree nut. This test looks for IgE, the allergy antibody, against it. It shows whether your immune system recognises it, not whether you are allergic.
Your immune system protects you by making antibodies, proteins that recognise things it sees as a threat.
In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
This test can help a doctor decide whether Walnut might be linked to symptoms such as hives, itching, swelling, tummy upset or wheezing after eating.

The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Walnut. It does not prove you will react to it.
Antibodies to Walnut were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
Little or no antibody to Walnut was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.
An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.
Do not cut Walnut or other foods from your diet based on this result alone. Unnecessary avoidance can limit nutrition, especially for children.
If you notice symptoms after eating Walnut, note what you ate, how much and how soon symptoms began. This helps a doctor judge whether the result matters.
Avoiding a food matters only if it causes symptoms. Many people with antibodies to a food eat it without any problem.
Talk to a doctor or allergy specialist if you get symptoms after eating Walnut.
Seek emergency care straight away for swelling of the face, eyes or tongue, a hoarse or whispered voice, trouble breathing or wheezing, dizziness or collapse after contact with any trigger.

Heart health describes how well your heart and blood vessels are likely to keep working over time. This assessment estimates your risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
Your heart pumps blood through a network of blood vessels to every part of your body.
Over years, cholesterol can build up as plaque inside artery walls, and high blood pressure can stiffen them.
Narrowed or blocked arteries can reduce blood flow to the heart or brain, which can lead to a heart attack or stroke.
Heart disease is one of the leading causes of illness and death, and it often develops silently for years.
Many of its main drivers, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and smoking, can be checked and managed.
Blood pressure: High pressure strains artery walls and the heart muscle over years.
Cholesterol: LDL and other plaque-forming particles build up in artery walls and narrow them.

Physical activity: Regular activity lowers blood pressure, improves cholesterol and helps the heart pump efficiently.

A predicted heart risk does not mean you have heart disease.
Normal cholesterol does not rule out heart risk, because blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history also matter.

Keep doing what protects your heart and blood vessels: regular movement, not smoking, meals built around vegetables, dal and whole grains, and checks of blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol at the interval your doctor suggests.

Cut back on salt, fried foods and packaged snacks, and add vegetables, dal and whole grains. This eating pattern is linked with healthier arteries.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Stopping smoking is one of the biggest single steps for heart health.
Know your blood pressure and get it checked regularly. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.

Cholesterol imbalance, also called dyslipidaemia, means the fats in your blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides, are at unhealthy levels.
Your blood carries fats inside particles such as LDL, HDL and VLDL.
Too much LDL or triglycerides, or too little HDL, makes it easier for fatty plaque to build up in arteries.
The build-up happens slowly and usually without symptoms.
Unhealthy blood fats are one of the main causes of heart attacks and strokes.
Unhealthy blood fats can be found with a simple blood test and are often improved with lifestyle and, when needed, treatment.
Foods high in saturated fat: Ghee, butter, cream, fatty meat and fried snacks lead the liver to clear less LDL.
Sugar and refined carbohydrates: Extra sugar and refined flour are turned into triglycerides by the liver.
Body weight: Extra weight, especially around the waist, raises triglycerides and lowers HDL.
Physical activity: Activity raises HDL and lowers triglycerides.
Inherited patterns: Genes shape how your liver makes and clears cholesterol.

A normal total cholesterol does not mean every blood fat is healthy.

High blood pressure, or hypertension, means blood is pushing too hard against the walls of your arteries for a long time.
Blood pressure is the force of blood on artery walls as your heart pumps.
When it stays high, the heart works harder and artery walls become strained and stiff.
Over time this damages blood vessels in the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes.
High blood pressure is very common and is a leading cause of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so measuring it is the only way to know.
Salt intake: Salt makes the body hold extra water, which raises pressure; pickles, papad, namkeen and processed foods add a lot.
Body weight: Extra weight makes the heart pump harder.
Physical activity: Regular activity lowers blood pressure over weeks.
Alcohol: Regular drinking raises blood pressure.
Stress and sleep: Ongoing stress and poor sleep keep pressure-raising hormones high.
Age and family history: Arteries stiffen with age, and high blood pressure runs in families.
You cannot tell your blood pressure by how you feel.
Normal kidney blood tests do not rule out high blood pressure.

Check your blood pressure at a pharmacy, clinic or at home every few months. It is the only way to know your numbers.
