Fatty liver means extra fat has built up inside your liver cells. The common form is now called MASLD, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, which replaced the older name NAFLD.
Your liver stores some fat, but too much can build up when the body takes in more energy than it uses.

Doctors call it MASLD when fat in the liver comes with metabolic risk factors, such as a large waist or extra weight, high blood sugar or type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, or high triglycerides or low HDL, and is not caused by heavy alcohol use.
When fat in the liver comes with inflammation and liver cell damage, it is called MASH, which replaced the older name NASH. Over years this can lead to scarring.
Fatty liver is very common and often silent.
Fatty liver is closely linked with type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides and heart disease, and early stages can improve with lifestyle change.

Insulin resistance or diabetes: When insulin works poorly, the liver stores more fat.

Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition where blood sugar stays too high, because the body does not respond well to insulin or does not make enough of it.
Insulin is a hormone that moves sugar from your blood into your cells for energy.
In type 2 diabetes, cells respond less to insulin. This is called insulin resistance.
The pancreas works harder to make more insulin, and over time it may not keep up, so blood sugar rises.
Type 2 diabetes is very common, especially in South Asia, and can develop silently for years.

Physical activity: Not being active is a risk factor for insulin resistance; activity helps manage blood sugar.
Diet: Sugary drinks, sweets and large portions of refined grains raise blood sugar and, over time, the load on insulin.

Family history: Diabetes in a parent or sibling raises your risk.
Age: Risk rises with age, though in India it often starts in the thirties and forties.

Extra weight around the waist raises the chance of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, fatty liver, heart disease and joint problems.

A normal BMI does not always mean healthy metabolism, especially for South Asians.

Replace sugary drinks and juices with water, buttermilk or unsweetened tea. Liquid sugar adds calories without filling you up.
Add movement through the day and some strength exercise twice a week. Muscle helps your body use sugar.

Thyroid health describes how well your thyroid gland, a small butterfly-shaped gland in your neck, is making the hormones that set your body's pace.
Your thyroid makes hormones called T4 and T3 that control how fast your body uses energy.
A signal from your brain, called TSH, tells the thyroid how much to make.
If the thyroid makes too little or too much, many body systems slow down or speed up.
Thyroid problems are common, especially in women, and can affect energy, weight, mood, periods, fertility and the heart.
Thyroid problems are easy to check with a blood test and usually treatable.
Autoimmune thyroid conditions: The immune system can attack the thyroid, making it underactive (Hashimoto) or overactive (Graves).
Family history: Thyroid conditions often run in families.
Iodine intake: The thyroid needs iodine; iodised salt prevents deficiency, while very large amounts can also upset the gland.
Pregnancy and after childbirth: Pregnancy changes thyroid needs, and some women develop thyroid inflammation after childbirth.
Some medicines: Medicines such as lithium and amiodarone can affect the thyroid.
Age and sex: Thyroid conditions are much more common in women and become more common with age.
Thyroid problems are not usually caused by diet.
A predicted thyroid risk does not mean your thyroid is not working.

Use iodised salt in normal amounts. Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones.
Most thyroid problems are caused by the immune system, not by lifestyle. Using iodised salt helps prevent iodine shortage.

Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is a common hormone condition that can make periods irregular, raise male-type hormones and affect how the body handles sugar.
Normally the ovaries release an egg each month.
In PCOS, hormone signals shift, so eggs may not be released regularly and periods become irregular.
The ovaries may make more androgens, male-type hormones that can cause acne or extra hair growth.
Many people with PCOS also have insulin resistance, which can raise blood sugar and weight.
PCOS is one of the most common hormone conditions in women of reproductive age.
PCOS can affect periods, fertility, skin, mood and long-term metabolic health.
Family history: PCOS runs in families, and a mother or sister with PCOS or type 2 diabetes raises the chance.

Regular activity, balanced meals and healthy sleep help insulin work better, which can improve PCOS symptoms.
PCOS also occurs in people of normal weight.
Talk to a doctor if your predicted risk is increased or very high, or if you have irregular periods, acne or extra hair growth, or difficulty getting pregnant.
See a doctor if you go three months or more without a period and are not pregnant.

It is not a diagnosis and does not measure the condition directly.

PCOS is linked with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, fatty liver, sleep apnoea, low mood and, with very infrequent periods, thickening of the womb lining.
Irregular, infrequent or missed periods.
Acne, oily skin, extra facial or body hair, or hair thinning on the scalp.
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight, and difficulty getting pregnant.
Oxidative stress is what happens when substances your cells make as they work build up faster than your body's protective systems can handle them.
Your cells naturally make some reactive molecules, often called free radicals, as they use energy.
Your body has protective systems, including antioxidants from food, that keep these molecules in balance.
When that protection cannot keep up, the extra molecules may damage parts of cells. That imbalance is called oxidative stress.
Over time, this imbalance can affect the health of cells.
Research discusses oxidative stress alongside inflammation and some longer-term health conditions.
Eating habits: Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains provide antioxidants that support the body's own protection.
Sleep: Sleep supports the body's repair processes.
Physical activity: Exercise makes some free radicals, but regular moderate activity strengthens the body's own protective systems.
Smoking: Smoke is one of the strongest outside sources of free radicals.
Ongoing stress: Long-term stress is linked with more oxidative strain.
Alcohol: Breaking down alcohol produces reactive molecules in the liver.
Air pollution and strong sunlight: Pollution and ultraviolet light create free radicals in the lungs and skin.
A normal blood report does not contradict a higher oxidative stress band, because routine blood tests do not measure it.
Antioxidant supplements have not been shown to prevent disease, and high-dose beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
This band is not a measurement of damage to your cells.
This score is a risk estimate, not a direct measurement of cell damage.
Not smoking, a varied diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit and dal, regular moderate activity and enough sleep support the body's own protective systems.
Include a variety of vegetables, fruit, pulses and other minimally processed foods. They provide natural antioxidants.
Keep a sleep routine that gives you enough rest. Sleep supports your body's repair processes.
Stay physically active in a way that fits your usual day. Regular moderate activity strengthens the body's own protective systems.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Smoking is a strong source of oxidative stress.
Smoking, heavy alcohol use, diets low in fruit and vegetables, and poor sleep are studied as general influences on oxidative stress.
There is no specific medical test or treatment for oxidative stress. Talk to a doctor if you have other raised risks or symptoms that worry you.

It is not a diagnosis and does not measure the condition directly.

Routine blood tests do not measure oxidative stress directly, and MetSights has not said exactly what this score predicts.
Research links long-term oxidative stress with inflammation and some conditions such as heart disease, but a score does not show that this has happened.
Oxidative stress does not cause symptoms you can feel.

Metabolic age is a Bio-AI estimate that MetSights presents as an age, to sum up parts of your metabolic health such as how your body handles sugar and fats. MetSights has not published how the number is calculated or what it is compared against.
Metabolic health is how well your body turns food into energy, keeps blood sugar steady and handles fats.
Your actual age is how many years you have lived. Metabolic age is an estimate based on health information, not a count of birthdays.

MetSights has not shared the formula, the weight given to each input or the group it compares you with, so the gap between your metabolic age and your real age cannot be read as a precise measure of anything.
Metabolic age is a simple way to start a conversation about blood sugar, blood fats, weight, activity and sleep.
The estimate does not measure how long you will live or how fast your whole body is ageing.
Physical activity: Activity helps the body use sugar and fats well.
Eating habits: Meals built around vegetables, pulses and whole grains support steadier blood sugar and blood fats.
Sleep: Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Body weight: Extra weight, especially around the waist, makes insulin and fat handling less efficient.
Blood sugar and blood fats: These are the measured parts of metabolic health that blood tests can show.
A higher metabolic age does not mean you have lost years of life.
A lower metabolic age does not guarantee good health.
Normal blood results can sit alongside a higher estimate, because a prediction is not a measurement.
No habit is promised to change the number by a set number of years.
Your measured results, such as HbA1c, fasting sugar and cholesterol, are a more reliable guide to where to focus than the metabolic age number.
The calculation method, inputs and reference group are not available, so CURA cannot say what produced your estimate.
Regular activity, balanced meals and enough sleep support metabolic health. Your measured results show where attention will help most.
Move regularly and include some strength exercise. Activity helps your body use sugar and fats.
Base meals on vegetables, pulses, whole grains and protein, with fewer sugary and fried foods. This supports steadier blood sugar and blood fats.
Keep a regular sleep routine. Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Activity, eating habits, sleep and weight are general influences on metabolic health. The provider has not said which inputs or weights it uses.
There is no medical treatment for metabolic age itself. Talk to a doctor about any raised blood sugar, cholesterol or other risks shown alongside it.
Metabolic age is an estimate from your Bio-AI assessment, not a measurement or diagnosis.
A different estimate on a later assessment can reflect changes in your health or in the information used.
Metabolic age is not linked to a specific disease. Metabolic health in general is linked with the risk of diabetes, fatty liver and heart disease.

That is the known general input set. The formula, feature weights and reference population are not available, and not every answer feeds every score.
Every heartbeat tells a story. Discover what yours can reveal.
Your heart is a muscle about the size of a fist that pumps blood around your body all day and night.
Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood out to every organ, and veins bring it back.
Cholesterol and other fats travel in the blood inside tiny particles. Some kinds, such as LDL, can slowly build up in artery walls and narrow them.
Narrowed arteries can reduce blood flow to the heart or brain, which is what causes most heart attacks and strokes.
Heart disease is a leading cause of death in India and often starts years before any symptom.
Blood fat tests, blood pressure and blood sugar together show how much strain your arteries are under.
Feeling fit does not mean arteries are healthy. High cholesterol and blood pressure usually cause no symptoms.
Regular movement, not smoking, meals built around vegetables, dal, whole grains and nuts, and modest salt protect your heart and arteries.
Blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and smoking add to each other, so improving any one of them lowers overall risk.
Heart disease in a parent or sibling at a young age is worth telling your doctor about.
From the food you eat to the energy you use, your liver does more than you think.
Your liver sits under your right ribs and is one of the busiest organs in the body.
Blood from your stomach and intestines passes through it, so it is the first stop for nutrients, medicines and alcohol.
It stores energy, makes proteins such as albumin, clears old red cells and breaks down medicines and alcohol.
It also makes bile, a fluid that drains through small tubes called bile ducts into the gut to help digest fat.
Liver problems are often silent until late, so blood tests are one of the few early signs.
About one in three Indian adults has fat in the liver, often without being overweight.
Normal liver tests do not rule out fatty liver.
Fatty liver is not only caused by alcohol.
Little or no alcohol, few sugary drinks and sweets, regular activity and a steady weight protect the liver.
Ask before starting herbal, weight-loss or bodybuilding supplements, because some can injure the liver.
Losing 3 to 5% of body weight can reduce liver fat, and activity helps even when weight does not change.
From your morning meals to your daily energy, there's more going on inside than you think.
When you eat, carbohydrates such as rice, roti and sugar are broken down into glucose, a sugar your cells use for energy.
Insulin, a hormone from the pancreas, moves glucose from the blood into muscle, fat and liver cells.
When these cells stop responding well to insulin, called insulin resistance, the pancreas has to make more, and blood sugar slowly rises.
Over years this can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
Indians tend to develop type 2 diabetes at younger ages and lower weights than many other groups.
Prediabetes is common and usually silent, and lifestyle change can delay or prevent diabetes.
You do not have to eat a lot of sweets to get diabetes. Genes, waist size, inactivity and refined grains all play a part.
Regular activity, meals built around vegetables, dal and whole grains, few sugary drinks and enough sleep help keep blood sugar healthy.
Waist size matters even if your weight looks normal.
If a parent or sibling has diabetes, regular blood sugar checks are worth it.
Your body's natural cleaning system works around the clock to keep things in balance.
You have two kidneys, each about the size of a fist, in your lower back.
Together they filter all your blood many times a day through about a million tiny filters, removing waste and extra water as urine.
They also balance salt, potassium and acid in the blood, help control blood pressure and help make red blood cells and keep bones strong.
Urine tests show what the kidneys let through, and blood tests such as creatinine and eGFR show how well they filter.
Kidney disease is often silent until a lot of function is lost.
Diabetes and high blood pressure are the commonest causes, so people with either need regular kidney checks.
Drinking huge amounts of water does not clean the kidneys. Enough to keep urine pale yellow is what helps.
Keep blood pressure and blood sugar healthy, drink water through the day and use painkillers such as ibuprofen only as advised.
Keeping salt low helps blood pressure and protects the kidney filters.
Feeling energetic or running low? Your blood may hold some clues.
Blood is made of red cells, white cells and platelets floating in a fluid called plasma.
Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, which needs iron, vitamin B12 and folate to be made.
White cells fight infection, and platelets help blood clot.
All three are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones, and a blood count shows how many of each you have.
Anaemia is very common in India, especially in women, and can cause tiredness and breathlessness.
Blood counts also help spot infection, inflammation and, less often, bone marrow problems.
Not every anaemia is from low iron. Thalassaemia trait, B12 shortage and long-term illness are common causes too.
Iron-rich foods such as dal, chana, green leafy vegetables, eggs or meat, eaten with a vitamin C food, help keep iron up.
Heavy periods are the commonest reason women run low on iron and are worth mentioning to a doctor.
Small nutrients make a big difference to the way you feel every day.
Vitamins and minerals are nutrients your body needs in small amounts to make blood, keep nerves and bones healthy and run chemical reactions.
Most come from food; vitamin D is mainly made in your skin in sunlight.
Some are stored in the body for months, such as B12 and vitamin D, so shortages build slowly.
Blood tests show the level in your blood, which does not always match stores inside cells.
Low vitamin D and low B12 are very common in India, including in people who eat well.
Shortages can cause tiredness, weak bones, tingling or anaemia.
More is not always better. Very large doses of vitamin D, for example, can cause nausea, kidney stones and kidney damage.
A varied diet with vegetables, fruit, dal, whole grains and dairy or eggs if you eat them, plus some daylight, covers most needs.
A tiny gland with a big influence on your energy, weight and everyday well-being.
Your thyroid is a small butterfly-shaped gland at the front of your neck.
It makes hormones, T4 and T3, that set how fast your body uses energy, affecting heart rate, temperature, weight, mood and periods.
The pituitary gland in the brain controls it by releasing TSH: more TSH when thyroid hormone is low, less when it is high.
The thyroid needs iodine, which iodised salt provides.
Thyroid conditions are common, especially in women, and are easy to test for and treat.
Untreated thyroid problems in pregnancy can affect the baby, so testing in pregnancy matters.
Thyroid problems are not only about weight. Tiredness, feeling cold or hot, hair, mood and periods can all change.
Thyroid conditions are not usually prevented by habits. Using iodised salt and having tests when you have symptoms, a family history or are pregnant is what helps.
Your body's natural defence system is always at work. Get to know it better.
Your immune system defends you against germs using white blood cells, antibodies and chemical signals.
Inflammation is part of that defence: blood flow, white cells and repair proteins rush to an injured or infected area.
Short-term inflammation helps healing, but low-grade inflammation that lasts for months is linked with heart disease and other long-term conditions.
Tests such as CRP and ESR show that inflammation may be present, but not where or why.
Inflammation markers help doctors follow infections and inflammatory conditions such as arthritis.
A raised marker during a recent cold is common and usually settles.
A normal ESR or CRP does not rule out every infection or inflammation.
Regular activity, not smoking, a healthy weight and a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains are linked with lower long-term inflammation.
Your hormones play a bigger role in your periods, skin and overall health than you might realise.
Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood that control growth, periods, fertility, energy and stress responses.
The pituitary gland in the brain directs many of them, including the ovaries, testes, thyroid and adrenal glands.
In women, LH and FSH from the pituitary drive the monthly cycle; in men, they drive testosterone and sperm production.
Hormone levels change with the time of day, the menstrual cycle, age and pregnancy, so timing matters for many tests.
Hormone tests help explain irregular periods, fertility problems, acne or extra hair, and low energy.
PCOS is one of the most common hormone conditions in Indian women.
One hormone result rarely gives a diagnosis on its own; timing and symptoms matter.
Regular sleep, activity and a steady weight support hormone balance.
Your bones support your body and store minerals.
Bones are living tissue that is constantly broken down and rebuilt.
They store most of the body's calcium and phosphate and release them when the blood needs more.
Vitamin D helps your gut absorb calcium, and parathyroid hormone keeps blood calcium steady.
Bone strength builds until about age 30, then slowly falls, faster in women after menopause.
Blood calcium shows the body's balance, not bone strength; a bone density scan measures strength.
A normal blood calcium does not mean bones are strong.
Calcium from milk, curd, ragi, sesame and green vegetables, enough vitamin D, and weight-bearing activity such as walking and strength exercise support bones.
Cells in your body make many different substances.
Some cells, including some cancer cells, release substances into the blood that labs can measure, called tumour markers.
Many non-cancer conditions, such as inflammation, infection and liver disease, raise these markers too.
They are mainly used to follow people already being treated for certain cancers, and sometimes to help investigate symptoms.
A raised tumour marker needs a doctor's assessment, but it does not mean cancer on its own.
Tumour markers are not screening tests for most people. A normal result does not rule out cancer.
Not smoking, limiting alcohol, staying active, a healthy weight and recommended cancer screening, such as cervical and breast checks, lower cancer risk more than marker tests do.
Sleep supports many everyday body processes.
During sleep your body repairs tissue, balances hormones and stores memories.
Short or poor sleep affects appetite hormones, blood sugar control, mood and blood pressure.
Blood tests do not measure sleep directly; questionnaire answers about sleep give context.
Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance and supports overall health.
Catching up on sleep at weekends does not fully undo short sleep during the week.
A regular bedtime and wake time, a dark quiet room and less screen time before bed help sleep.
Your immune system usually protects you from harmful things.
Your immune system usually ignores harmless things such as food, dust and pollen.
In allergy, it makes an antibody called IgE against one of these, which can trigger sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing on contact.
Having IgE to something, called sensitisation, does not always mean you react to it.
Allergy tests help a doctor link symptoms to triggers, but they are read with what actually happens when you are exposed.
A positive allergy test is not proof of allergy, and cutting foods based on tests alone can harm nutrition, especially in children.
There's more to your health story. Explore the other pieces of the puzzle.

A low haemoglobin with a low ferritin confirms iron-deficiency anaemia; a low ferritin with normal haemoglobin shows stores running low before anaemia starts.
Ferritin reflects stored iron; serum iron reflects iron circulating at collection.
A low iron with a normal ferritin may be a timing effect or inflammation, because serum iron changes hour to hour.

A high saturation with a high ferritin can point to iron overload; a high ferritin with normal saturation more often reflects inflammation or fatty liver.

HDL and LDL carry cholesterol in different particles; both add context to artery risk.
A good HDL does not cancel out a high LDL. Doctors focus on LDL first when deciding on treatment.
Triglycerides are circulating energy fats and add context to the cholesterol pattern.
High triglycerides with low HDL is a common pattern in South Asians and often goes with insulin resistance; the two usually improve together with less sugar and more activity.
Total cholesterol includes HDL cholesterol. HDL helps carry cholesterol back to the liver.
A high total with a high HDL can be a healthier pattern than a high total with a low HDL, so the total means little until HDL is known.
Creatinine is used to estimate how quickly your kidneys filter blood.
eGFR is calculated from creatinine, so a muscular person with high creatinine may get a falsely low eGFR.
Urea and creatinine are wastes removed by your kidneys. Their production differs.
Urea rises with dehydration and protein much more than creatinine does, so comparing them helps tell dehydration from reduced filtering.
Fasting sugar is a single measurement; HbA1c reflects sugar levels over several weeks.
When fasting sugar and HbA1c both sit in the prediabetes range they confirm each other; when they disagree, a doctor may repeat one or use another test.
Insulin helps regulate sugar; its fasting level can add context to glucose patterns.
A normal HbA1c with a high insulin can mean insulin resistance before blood sugar rises.

A low TSH with a high T3 fits an overactive thyroid.
TSH tells your thyroid to produce hormones, and T4 feeds back to regulate TSH.
A high TSH with a low T4 points to an underactive thyroid; a high TSH with a normal T4 is called subclinical and is often rechecked.

Vitamin D affects calcium absorption, which influences PTH release.
A high PTH with low vitamin D usually means the body is compensating, and often settles once vitamin D is corrected.

Low vitamin D can lower phosphate as well as calcium.

A low haemoglobin with a low MCH fits iron shortage or thalassaemia trait.

Long unbroken sitting is linked with poorer blood sugar control and heart health, separate from how much exercise you do. Getting up to move every half hour or so helps.
Daily physical activity helps your body manage blood sugar, lowers blood pressure and improves cholesterol. A blood sugar reading after a walk is often lower than before.
Leisure exercise and sport across the week add to daily movement; regular activity lowers the risk of insulin resistance and supports the heart.
Higher-intensity activity improves fitness and blood sugar handling more per minute than gentle activity, though any regular movement helps.
Walking is the most common activity for Indian adults and helps blood sugar, blood pressure and weight, especially after meals.
Regular sport adds activity that supports blood sugar control and heart fitness.
Enough good-quality sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance; short sleep is linked with weight gain and higher blood sugar.
Alcohol is broken down by the liver, so regular drinking can raise GGT, AST and ALT and push triglycerides up. Stopping or cutting down lets these improve.
Smoking damages artery linings, lowers HDL and makes blood more likely to clot; stopping lowers heart risk within a few years.

Red meat is a rich source of iron and B12 that the body absorbs easily.
Eating fruit and vegetables every day supplies vitamin C, which helps the body absorb iron from dal, greens and grains.
Fresh fruit such as amla, guava and oranges supplies vitamin C, which helps absorb plant iron when eaten with meals.
Fresh vegetables supply vitamin C and folate; long cooking destroys some vitamin C.
Biscuits, cakes and white bread are made from refined flour, which raises blood sugar quickly and, eaten often, adds to the load on insulin and to liver fat.
Sugary drinks and desserts raise blood sugar quickly; NIDDK advises limiting simple sugars for fatty liver, and lifestyle change can delay type 2 diabetes.
Tea or coffee with added sugar adds sugar several times a day without feeling like a sweet; unsweetened tea and coffee do not.
The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones, and iodised salt is the main source in India.
Extra salt makes the body hold water, which raises blood pressure; pickles, papad and namkeen add a lot of hidden salt too.
Butter, ghee and cream are rich in saturated fat, which leads the liver to clear less LDL from the blood.
Red meat, especially fatty cuts and processed meat, adds saturated fat that can raise LDL.
When you drink little water, the kidneys save water and make concentrated urine, which raises specific gravity and can make kidney blood results read higher.
Body weight gives context for blood sugar, blood pressure and liver fat, because extra weight makes insulin work less well.
Waist size reflects fat around the abdomen, which is closely linked with insulin resistance, fatty liver and heart risk, even at a normal weight.
Body fat percentage shows how much of your weight is fat rather than muscle.
Systolic pressure is the top number: the pressure when your heart beats. A high top number strains arteries, heart and kidneys over years.
Diastolic pressure is the bottom number: the pressure between beats. A high bottom number also strains arteries over time.

A condition you have already been diagnosed with changes how results are read, for example blood sugar targets in diabetes.
Medicines change many results, for example statins lower LDL and some blood pressure tablets change potassium, so knowing them avoids misreading a result.
